speechtext:
I rise to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether the Government intends to make changes in the Wheat Board act, and whether the Minister of Forestry in the speech which he was kind enough to send me was expressing Government policy when he said:
The policy of the Canadian Wheat Board cannot be regarded as a national farm policy.
And further:
The Canadian Wheat Board is therefore using its powers for strictly regional purposes.
And later on:
If we are to change the present feed grains policy, we have two options before us: either the Canadian Wheat Board relinquishes its wide powers over what happens to feed grains in Canada, in exchange for a gradual abandonment of freight assistance for grains shipped to eastern Canada, or the Prairie producers will have to resign themselves to seeing the eastern feeders set up an effective countervailing agency. Since acceptance of
June 17, 1965

Inquiries of the Ministry the first option seems highly unlikely for the time being, the setting up of an agency in eastern Canada with wide powers, plus a system of equalization payments based on the difference in price between the two grain markets, seems to offer an alternative worth considering.
Is the Government in agreement with this speech? Does it agree with the view that the wheat board "juggles with delivery quotas, adjusts interim payments and regulates the allotment of freight cars, and has sometimes been able to bring about an artificial rationing of feed grain availabilities at the Lake-head"? Does this speech represent the view of the Government, and does the Government intend to attack the wheat board in this way, an attack that has not been made against that body for as far back as I remember?

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce could give the House some information with respect to the International Wheat Agreement. I understand that the present agreement, which expires on July 31 this year, is to be extended for one year, and that the United States Senate has just ratified the extension in so far as that country is concerned. Has Canada signed an extension? Will this matter be referred to the House of Commons? If it has not been signed by the Government of Canada, is it the Government's intention to sign it fairly soon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my recollection is that I announced in this House that it was the Government's intention to agree to an extension for one year. There are no changes
June 17, 1965

Inquiries of the Ministry in the provisions of the international wheat agreement; the provisions are simply to be extended for another year. At that time I expressed the hope that the United States would ratify the extension, and it has done so.
There will be an opportunity, I hope very soon, for the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce to be brought forward for discussion, at which time there will be an opportunity to examine me and members of the Canadian Wheat Board.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Are meetings now going to be held with respect to either a new agreement or a further extension after the expiration of the present agreement, which will expire on July 31, 1966? Has the Minister any hope that there will be any change in the price range?

Mr. Speaker, the international wheat agreement was not renegotiated but was simply extended for another year because of the discussions now going on in Geneva concerning a cereals agreement which will comprehend not only wheat but other grains. It was because of those discussions which were proceeding currently that it was decided that it would not be in order to attempt to renegotiate the international wheat agreement itself. We are hopeful, indeed I can give the assurance, that there will be an agreement in effect before the present international wheat agreement expires.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I did not give this reply earlier. I had intended to give it yesterday but my hon. friend was unavoidably absent, I am sure on public business.
Hon. We shall have more to say about this later.
There has been a great deal of discussion about the clause which deals with newspapers and the proposal to retain Canadian ownership of Canadian newspapers. Some have said that the freedom of the press is involved in this proposal. I cannot agree with that at all. If we consider what the freedom of the press means we can only conclude that it means freedom to print editorials and news stories without government interference or censorship of any kind. And it presumably includes freedom to establish publications in the country. In practice the latter freedom is severely restricted by economics, as I am sure the owners of the Vancouver Times would testify. Their venture has already cost them about $1J million and the future of the publication is not at all certain.
Essentially, freedom of the press must mean freedom to print what is desired without
June 17, 1965

interference. I cannot see that this is affected by the proposal before us. Certainly the freedom to sell Canadian newspapers to nonCanadian owners is interfered with, but this is a very different matter from what we generally understand as being the freedom of the press.
I feel the term "freedom of the press" is much abused. In many cases it merely means that the press is as free as the publisher of the paper wants it to be. In Canada many newspapers are personally controlled by their publishers, and these newspapers do exactly what their publishers want them to do. For example Mr. Bassett, the owner of the Toronto Telegram, is quite free to call the present Leader of the Opposition Canada's greatest Prime Minister one year to turn against him the next. He is free to publish the column written by my hon. friend from Port Arthur or to kill it at any time he wishes. The same applies to the contributions by Mr. Lubor Zink. The former publisher of the Ottawa Citizen was quite free to let his editorial staff determine the paper's editorial policy; it was rather to the left of centre. But when the new publisher took over he was free to get rid of that editorial staff and establish an editorial policy the effect of which was to make the paper almost an organ of the Liberal party. The former publisher of the Vancouver Sun was free to run editorials supporting the Liberal party, but he was also free to suggest to his reporters that they should write stories at election times in favour of Liberal candidates. The publishers of La Presse were quick to fire Mr. Pelletier when they did not agree with the editorials he was writing. It is true these are probably bad examples, and I am not suggesting that all Canadian newspapers act in this way.
How free do publishers want to be? They have the freedom to run their papers in any way they please, and the public be damned. This is increasingly true, I suggest, in cities which have only one newspaper, an increasingly common circumstance today.
I object to being presented with this omnibus resolution which includes so many things -income tax reductions for most taxpayers, exemptions dealing with dependants, trade union dues, mineral exploration, important principles dealing with the press, and so on. The opposition is placed in the position of voting either for or against the whole package. This may be smart politics, but it is a poor way of transacting public business.
The proper way to handle this would be to take certain important clauses out of the
Income Tax Act
resolution and allow the committee to debate them separately. The clause dealing with periodicals should be debated separately, and the clause dealing with newspapers should be debated and voted upon separately. I think if given the opportunity to vote on these items separately, members of this party would support the provision suggested by the Minister concerning ownership of Canadian newspapers. However, during such a discussion I believe some members could propose other methods of handling this particular problem.
I am sure the Minister has received a copy of the Winnipeg Free Press of yesterday with its editorial, as have other Members of the House. If he thought the hon. Member for Port Arthur was rough with him the other night he should read that issue of the Free Press, in which the words "outright falsehood" are used. I do not intend to quote the whole of this editorial, but there is one part of it I should like to draw to the committee's attention:
Mr. Gordon knows full well that there are a number of practical alternatives to the advertising tax which are equally effective and far less dangerous. One (proposed by F.P. Publications) would involve voluntary renunciation by newspapers of the right to transfer their shares to nonresidents. Another would have Parliament simply declare, by resolution, its intention to prohibit take-overs should they occur. Still another would be to invite the provinces, which have constitutional power over property and civil rights, to introduce their own legislation forbidding foreign ownership of the press.
I am not sure that this would be as effective as the measure which is proposed, but they are certainly alternatives and perhaps these, as well as others which hon. Members might like to propose, could be voted on. We cannot do that as long as we are dealing with this legislation in what I would have to call this rather tricky manner of including everything in the one resolution.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that it may be a smart political move, but it is a very poor way to transact public business. The effect of it will only be to make the whole resolution much more difficult of passage. I would like the Minister to bear this in mind, because Members are placed in the position of opposing certain items and supporting others. But we do intend to put up a fight on those items to which we are very strongly opposed.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take the time of the committee for only a short period in order to make some comments on this resolution which precedes

June 17, 1965*
Income Tax Act
a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. I do not intend to spread my remarks over all the items in this package of amendments proposed to the Income Tax Act; I shall confine my remarks to two items that are in the resolution.
Prior to doing that I want to express my disappointment with regard to an omission from the resolution. I refer to the failure to relieve from corporation taxes private corporations engaged in the production and distribution of power. I think this is an opportunity the Minister and the Government should have taken, because here in my judgment we have a discriminatory tax. After all, these private corporations operate in a field in which many provincial Crown corporations also operate; they are providing the same service. Although they are not usually in direct competition with each other, they are nevertheless supplying a service to the Canadian people.
The nature of their industry is such that due to the fact that they have no competition in their field, they are a monopoly in the area in which they operate and are therefore controlled by provincial utilities commissions. This produces the result that Canadian citizens in areas served by private corporations supplying the public utilities are subject to a tax to which Canadian citizens in other areas are not subject. This of course creates a situation where there is tremendous pressure on Provincial Governments to take over privately owned public utilities and transfer them into provincially owned Crown corporations. This is a situation that cannot be justified from any purely logical point of view.
I am not one who maintains that public utilities should necessarily be publicly owned. I think there are cases where it is in the general interest that they be publicly owned, but on the other hand I think there are cases where services of this sort can be operated perhaps more efficiently by private industry. The two methods should be judged on their merits; and one method, namely private ownership in this case, should not be burdened with an artificial load which happens to fall on it and its clients because of an anomaly in the income tax structure.
For example, in my own province of Prince Edward Island the power is provided by a privately owned corporation in most cases. This means there are extra taxes going into the federal treasury from Prince Edward Island which are part of the individual cit-

izen's light bill in that area. This would not be the case if it were a provincial Crown corporation. This to me is completely unfair from any logical point of view, and the Minister should have taken the opportunity to correct this anomaly.
I now wish to refer briefly to paragraph 10, in which reference is made to certain items of expenditure that now can be claimed as an expense by taxpayers. I refer to (d) and more particularly to (c), which says:
That there may he deducted in computing the income of a taxpayer an amount in respect of an outlay or expense made by the taxpayer in the 1965 and subsequent taxation years
(c)	for clearing land or laying tile drainage for the purpose of carrying on a farming business,
Subparagraph (b) also provides for such a deduction in respect of landscaping property used by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income. I presume that both these things would apply to farms; that is landscaping and clearing land or laying tile drainage. This is a very small step in the right direction, I believe, and I commend the Minister for taking it. I regret, however, that it will have very little application and therefore the beneficial effects flowing from it will be minor indeed; because I think it will apply only in isolated cases. It will only provide an incentive to landscape or clear land where the operation is already a profitable one, sufficiently profitable to be taxable under the Income Tax Act. But the greatest problem, as far as agriculture is concerned, in this field is that many operators do not have an economic unit; it is too small to be economic and therefore is not profitable. It is these people who need most to enlarge their acreage of land under cultivation, and there will be no incentive for them to do so.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that we should give careful consideration to the importance of keeping our agricultural land in Canada in such condition that it is potentially productive even though it is not in production at the present time. We should keep it in such a state that it can be readily made productive in the very near future. I am convinced that within very tew years, probably in this decade, agricultural surpluses will become a thing of the past, and that the full impact of the world population explosion will begin to hit the productive capacity of North America as it has long since hit the productive capacity of more highly populated countries.
I think in this circumstance it is wasteful from a national point of view that large
June 17. 1965

acreages of our productive agricultural land should be going out of production permanently due to temporary conditions. A great deal of suitable agricultural land is being used up every day for the development of residential and commercial areas, airports and things of that sort. But this is not all. There are vast acreages of good agricultural land in Canada that have been abandoned because the units in which it has been operated up to the present time have not been economic.
[DOT] (3:30 pjm.)
In this connection I would refer to the Province of Prince Edward Island. There are vast acreages of farms there which have been abandoned over the years because of the economic conditions in agriculture which have existed over a long period of time. These abandonments have also been caused through the inability of the owners of these farms to acquire the necessary capital and markets to operate them as economic units. I am sure the situation is the same in other parts of Canada.
This is an appalling state of affairs, because this agricultural land is growing up in scrub and bush and becoming almost worthless, producing nothing of value. If it were growing up in valuable timber this would prove a long term asset, but in this case this land grows up in scrub, becoming unsuitable for agricultural use except at great cost for clearing and so on. This situation is more widespread than is generally realized by the public, I think.
In Prince Edward Island agriculture is the main industry, the backbone of our whole economy. Our only other important industries are the fisheries and tourism, but agriculture is far more important than they are, relatively speaking. In this regard I should like to quote from "Land Utilization in Prince Edward Island", which is Geographical Memoir No. 9 published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The following is a quotation from page 49:
Between 1911 and 1956 the Island's acreage of improved agricultural land decreased from 769,140 acres to 645,492 acres, or by approximately 16 per cent. Since all but a small proportion of this contraction has occurred since 1931, and as much as 74 per cent between 1941 and 1951, much of the abandoned acreage has had insufficient time to revert to forest growth.
I might say that most of it will never revert to forest growth which will have any value.
I think this provision is a tentative step toward recognizing the need for farmers to be in a position to bring more potentially good
Income Tax Act
agricultural land into production, but it will not touch the heart of the problem. I would most strongly suggest that the Minister point out this question to his colleagues the Minister of Forestry and the Minister of Agriculture, because something much more than this minor assistance must be given before there is any appreciable benefit.
I now wish to turn for a few moments to another item in this omnibus resolution. I refer to paragraph 19, which reads in part as follows:
In computing income, no deduction shall be made in respect of an otherwise deductible outlay or expense of a taxpayer for advertising space in an issue of a non-Canadian newspaper or periodical dated after December 31, 1965 for an advertisement directed primarily to a market in Canada.
Then it goes on to define what is a Canadian publication and what are the exceptions; and the following paragraphs Canadianize- artificially, I think-Reader's Digest and Time magazine. I not only object to the detail of the matter; I object most strenuously to this approach to the problem. It is dangerous when a government takes the attitude that it can judge which freedoms can be encroached upon with impunity, especially in view of the necessity for the complete freedom of the press. By that I do not mean licence, but the complete freedom of the press to criticize, and to criticize especially actions of governments where the press think it is suitable to do so. This is something which should not be tampered with in any way either directly or indirectly.
In his remarks the other evening the Minister expressed the opinion that no strong opposition had been taken to his measure by the Canadian press. To refute this, Mr. Chairman, I would merely quote from an editorial which appeared in yesterday's Toronto Telegram which I think summed it up well. It says in part:
The Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association unanimously passed a resolution condemning the Gordon proposal and sent a delegate to Prime Minister Pearson urging the abandonment of this legislation.
Freedom of the press is at stake in this issue, in spite of Mr. Gordon's protestations to the contrary. It always has been.
The whole principle of protecting Canadian publications-periodical or daily-through legislative manipulation is odious. It touches the question of press independence, one of the pillars of a free society.
I agree wholeheartedly with this point of view. I object to the other items and details contained in the proposal, but I object most strongly of all to this particular principle. Therefore I would strongly urge the Minister

June 17, 1965

Mr. Chairman, my comments concerning the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act will be rather short.
A while ago we had the opportunity of saying a few words on this, and I do not intend to repeat what was said then. On the other hand, I find it odd that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who introduces these amendments, did not take into account our representations when the resolution was before us for the first time.
For instance, last year difficulties were encountered with regard to receipts for charitable donations throughout the province of Quebec and Canada. Income tax inspectors burst into rectories and called on clergymen to enquire about the accuracy of charitable donations receipts. Please note that according to the act, a Canadian citizen has the right to deduct up to a maximum of 10 per cent for charitable donations. And yet the department does not accept from a taxpayer receipts not exceeding 10 per cent of his income.
Last year these receipts were reduced to their simplest expression, namely $100, amount which any Canadian taxpayer has the right to claim without producing receipts. Someone produced receipts totalling $500 and it was reduced by $400 to $100.
This year, instead of changing the situation, a basic deduction of 10 per cent is proposed. This is an amendment which will help those having a high income but Canadian workers will gain no advantage on the whole. I ask the Minister of Finance this: instead of providing that charitable donations may be deducted up to a maximum of 10 per cent, thus leading the taxpayer to believe that he is entitled to deduct the maximum of 10 per cent of his income, why not reduce the rate to 6 per cent and tell him that he may deduct this amount without having to produce receipts?

Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with the Income Tax Act and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), only the Minister of Finance is empowered to amend this act. When we discuss it, the Minister tells us that to speak about the income tax is to go beyond the scope of those items.
Mr. Chairman, section 1 introduces an amendment providing that for the 1966 and subsequent taxation years the income tax payable by an individual be reduced by an amount equal to the lesser of 10 per cent of basic tax or $600 and for the 1965 taxation year by an amount equal to the lesser of 5 per cent of basic tax or $300.
I said a while go that the minister was not helping the Canadian workers with this 10 per cent reduction of the basic tax. If the Minister of Finance had, for example, moved an amendment providing that incomes less than $5,000 for married persons and $2,500 for single persons would be exempted from income tax, then he would have helped all Canadian workers.
I would like to point out that under this new legislation, those earning high salaries will profit more from it, but low income groups will not profit from it at all. The federal members of Parliament will profit from this legislation, since our taxable income will be reduced by 10 per cent, out of
June 17, 1965

our income of $12,000 per year and we will thus save about $350 or $375 per year on income tax. But our fellow citizens, our electors in our respective ridings, will get hardly anything out of it.
Mr. Chairman, there is something else. The Minister of Finance should have added another amendment to that act to allow workers, for instance, to deduct from their income the cost of the tools they need to work and do their job.
If a lawyer buys something for his office, furniture, for instance, his bookkeeper deducts the cost of it from his income tax. If a doctor buys some equipment, scalpels or something else, he is allowed to deduct the cost from his income; he can get an income tax deduction for those amounts. As the owner of a garage, if I buy equipment for it, I can deduct it from my income.
But the worker who has to buy for $800, $900, $1,500, or $2,000 of equipment, the carpenters, the mechanics, those people are not entitled to deduct from their income the cost of the tools which they need to do their job.
Why did the Minister of Finance not take into account our suggestions, while preparing those amendments to the Income Tax Act. Had he done so, he would have helped, thousands of Canadian workers.
In conclusion, I shall say-I have often said it before I repeat again-that the legislation introduced by the Minister of Finance allows the rich to grow richer, though fewer and the poor to grow poorer and to multiply. It seems that the government and its ministers always come up with this kind of legislation.
Therefore, I suggest to the Minister of Finance to consider seriously the possibility of stabilizing, for instance, the percentage in respect of receipts for charitable donations. The basic exemption should be increased to $5,000 for married men and $2,500 for single persons. This would permit those in the lower income brackets to enjoy some advantages and workers should be allowed to deduct from their income amounts spent for purchasing the tools they need to work at their trades. Then, they would not have to pay heavy taxes on the equipment they need to do their work.
Mr. Chairman, there are several other important points besides those I have mentioned. There is for instance the provision under which a nephew, a niece or another dependant may finally be recognized as human beings. We approve the good points of this measure.

We would like the government and the minister of Finance to be more generous and fair for those who need it most, that is the Canadian worker, the Canadian farmer, in short, the people of Canada.

I have another reason for speaking today on this particular matter. The proposed change in the Income Tax Act as envisaged in section 19 of the resolution is, as has been pointed out by others, the beginning of an attack on the freedom of the press. The Minister cannot brush this aside by any casual statement such as he gave us on Tuesday. He cannot convince us, and I do not think he can convince the Canadian people, that this Liberal Government, as he said in the course of his remarks, "would never contemplate any measure which could seriously be construed as interfering with the freedom of the press". We do not have that confidence in this Government; and any confidence the people of Canada had in the Government two years ago has been dissipated over the course of the period since then.
The reason that confidence has been dissipated is the lack of information supplied to

One of my reasons for losing confidence in the Prime Minister emerged last year during the course of the flag debate, when on three different occasions he stated in the House that "none of us saw a Canadian red ensign in those years", referring to the first world war. That statement was refuted by our late friend Hon. George Nowlan and by myself, both of us having served in France during that period. But despite that denial by serving soldiers who had been there and who saw that Canadian flag, the Prime Minister repeated that statement in the House, on three occasions although he himself, of course, was not present in France. That is one of the reasons I cannot place any confidence in statements made by the Prime Minister.
We are accustomed to evasion time after time in the House when we ask questions. We are subjected to evasion on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs-I am sorry he is not here-who on six or seven different occasions has evaded the question when I have asked him what the Government is doing about its promise to negotiate out of the use of nuclear arms. He has engaged in evasion instead of simply saying no, we have not done anything about it, which would be the truthful answer.
I get evasive answers from the Minister of National Defence. Only last week I inquired whether our Voodoo planes in Canada are equipped with nuclear missiles. His answer was that they are fully operational, which was

an evasion of the question, instead of saying either yes or no. Today we had an example in the case of the Minister of Labour. So it goes down the line.
But the situation has become very serious with regard to the Minister of Finance. He has been attacked by very prominent Canadian newspapers, and I think he must make a statement to the House with regard to these attacks. He has been accused in words that we are not allowed to use in the House. He has been accused of falsehood. His statements are called untrue, and these accusations are broadcast throughout the country. When newspapers of the standing of the Globe and Mail and the Winnipeg Free Press make such accusations against a Minister of the Crown the situation becomes extraordinarily serious. These are not accusations such as are sometimes made in the heat of debate in this chamber, but are accusations made by responsible newspapers. What answer is the Minister going to give to these accusations? In an editorial in the Globe and Mail of June 16 these words appear:
Finance Minister Walter Gordon suffers either from a bad memory inexcusable in a Minister of the Crown, or he is tampering with the truth.
What stronger statement could be made? There is a stronger statement in the editorial, which quotes these words from the speech of the Minister on June 14, as found on page 2386 of Hansard:
-this had not aroused opposition or suggestions that it posed a threat to the freedom of the press when it was to be applied to periodicals. It has been surprising, therefore, that this charge should be raised when the same principle is now to be applied to newspapers. It is difficult to accept the fact that a principle can be right and good, and widely accepted as such, when applied to one field of communications but not when it is applied to another.
What does the Globe and Mail say? These are the words of the Globe and Mail of June 16:
Mr. Gordon's statement is false.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is indeed very serious. What is the Minister of Finance going to do? The people of Canada have read that statement in the Globe and Mail. Are they going to place any further reliance on statements made by the Minister of Finance? The editorial in the Globe and Mail goes on to point out that that newspaper had expressed opposition to the proposals time after time, going back to the proposals with regard to periodicals in 1961. Yet the Minister says that it has not aroused opposition, or sugges-

This is the exact opposite of the truth. The Government's proposal asserts, for the first time, the Government's right to impose discriminatory taxation on advertising by defining who shall and who shall not be entitled to tax exemption.
This is what is contained in the Government's proposal. The Minister went on to say, as reported at page 2386 that it "provides no precedent for any kind of Government interference in the complete freedom of the press". I am prepared to accept the statement made by the Winnipeg Free Press in respect of this matter-"Again a complete falsehood". And those are not my words; they are the words of the Winnipeg Free Press.
[The Acting Chairman (Mr. Cameron, High Park).]
The legislation does set a precedent, and a most dangerous precedent at that. Having asserted for the first time a Government's right to tax advertising on a basis of ownership there is nothing to prevent extension on other bases.
That is a statement which I accept as a reply to the Minister's earlier statement. Then the hon. gentleman went on to say-and again his words may be found in Hansard-that no practical alternative had been found despite careful thought and much discussion with the people concerned. Well, alternatives were suggested. The Winnipeg Free Press put forward quite a number before this resolution came before us for debate.
I can mention three which have been drawn to my attention. It was suggested that the Government might urge all newspapers to voluntarily forfeit the right to their own alienation through the sale of their voting stock. That was one suggestion. Another suggestion was that the Government might declare any foreign purchase of a Canadian newspaper to be null and void. The Free Press made a further suggestion. It said if the Government were to introduce a formal resolution in Parliament to the effect that in no circumstances would the alienation of Canadian newspapers be allowed, and that if necessary retroactive legislation would be passed to deal with such a situation, such a resolution would receive unanimous or virtually unanimous approval. Then, trying to win the attention of the Prime Minister, the paper suggested that if the Prime Minister would proclaim in the name of Parliament and the whole of the Canadian nation a solemn embargo on the foreign control of communications media, all foreigners would understand.
These are alternatives which have been suggested, but the Minister brushed them all aside and said that no practical alternative had been found. I think these are practical alternatives. The Minister himself gave us an example, reference to which will be found on page 2386. He was very proud of the announcement he made last September the effect of which was retroactive to the time of the earlier statement he made in September of 1964, with regard to the acquisition of any of our chartered banks by people not resident in Canada.
There are two points at issue here. One is the maintenance of the freedom of the press, which is just as important to the Canadian people as is the maintenance of freedom of speech in this Chamber. We feel this proposal would be an encroachment on the freedom of the press. It is our duty to protect the
June 17. 1985

Canadian people against any such encroachment. We are not satisfied with assurances that this particular government would, of course, not do anything which might interfere with press freedom, an expression merely of good intentions on the part of this administration.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that there is no longer any confidence in this House or throughout Canada with regard to the good intentions of this Government. There is too much evasion, too much withholding of information, and a regrettable lack of frankness in this Chamber. Here is the culminating point. We find the Minister of Finance accused by leading newspapers in this country of not telling the facts, of not giving the truth. They use the word "falsehood" with regard to his statements.
This, I say, is a most serious thing. It is one of the most serious things which have occurred in the last two years and which have come to our attention. The Minister of Finance, one of the most powerful figures in the Cabinet, close adviser to the Prime Minister, is accused by leading newspapers in this country of falsifying the record. I think there is only one course open to that Minister, and that is for him to submit his resignation.
Oh, oh.

There is little I can add to what has been said by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre. However, while I have been sitting here my mail came in and it does carry strong support for the views expressed a moment ago by my hon. friend.
This Government has made the telling of partial truths the cornerstone of Government policy. We have had example after example, particularly in the last few months, of Ministers giving us but part of the truth. We had an example this afternoon from the Minister of Labour. I do not understand it. I cannot conceive that giving answers which are not truthful is any mark of forensic capacity or of ministerial responsibility in this Chamber.
We had an example a couple of weeks ago in connection with the action being taken by the Government to bring in a new social security card. I had certain information. I brought it before the House. It had to do with the removal of the coat of arms of Canada from the card and the substitution of a single maple leaf. The answer I received was evasive. The information I had was that objection was being raised in parts of Canada

to having a coat of arms because it had the crown and the union jack on it. I had that direct information, because I do not ask questions in the House of Commons unless I have reasonable ground for knowing what the answer will be.
But they do not learn over there. When I have asked questions and those questions have been evaded, it has not been very long before the truth has come out showing that the questions were well based. But they cannot learn. One does not expect some of the Parliamentary Secretaries to learn; that would be expecting too much. But I knew this was a fact. The answer was evasive. First the Minister of Labour said, in effect, "There is nothing to it". Well, they have come out with it now. They had to admit it.

Now that card bears the strongest possible resemblance to the membership card of the Liberal Party organization in Canada. The removal of the coat of arms and the substitution therefor of the maple leaf produces a card that bears a striking resemblance to that denoting membership in the Liberal Party.
The point I make is this. This Government does not give Parliament the facts. The Prime Minister-and I am not going to deal with him in his absence; I have dealt with him in his presence on this-told Parliament last November that he had no information regarding the connection of an executive assistant with alleged bribery. Freedom of the press.

What further evidence do you need to support the contention that what this Government has tried to do, is bring about thought control in Canada, destroy political opponents, malign them by means of mercenary publicists who peer in keyholes or invent in the darkness of their offices. Imagine the alertness shown by the Hansard people. We have not yet had an explanation from the Minister of Public Works, and I should like to hear from him what happened. What would hon. gentlemen

opposite have said when we were in office if one of the greatest thugs engaged in narcotics distribution had been so signally-honoured as to have been raised by the Department of Public Works to the status of minister on a document of Parliament, elevated to the Privy Council, indeed the Cabinet itself?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Now, Sir, what is the reaction to this legislation? I know the Government has tried to tell us that this is the same legislation as that which was recommended by the O'Leary Commission. It is nothing of the kind. The O'Leary Commission made no recommendations about newspapers. It endeavoured to preserve Canada's periodicals against unjust competition by Time and Reader's Digest and other United States magazines which have masqueraded as Canadian, establishing themselves in Canada in a preferred position to Canadian magazines endeavouring to retain a Canadian identity.
I speak of Maclean's magazine, Chatelaine and the like. We wanted to see something which was Canadian preserved so that Canadian opinion would be available. We said if these people can come into Canada from the United States with what I call ready print or ready prepared editorial content or other content against which Canadian magazines cannot compete, then this matter is far removed from the question of newspapers. This was at the request of Canadian periodical publishers, it being the only course for their preservation as national entities within Canada.
Who asked for the present legislation? Nobody. Why do the Government want it? They must have a reason. They published tremendous advertisements in the press during the last few days giving the detail of the redistribution of seats in the provinces as an attempted sop to the great newspapers of Canada. After all, they said, here is a quarter of a million we will let you have. They thought they could buy silence with that.
What is going to be the reaction to this legislation in other parts of the world? We have already had one reaction from the International Press Institute meeting in London. Sean MacBride, Secretary General of the International Commission of World Jurists, quoted Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, as proclaimed by the United Nations, in a speech he made within the last week. That declaration says:

Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression. This right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.
This is the most important right guaranteed to human beings, and, as he said in his speech, it must be preserved.
What is behind this, Mr. Chairman? I have seen this Government throttling opinion, pressuring people by the subtleties of modern propaganda, covering up facts relating to matters before Parliament. It is the strangest thing today, but a matter is reported on one page of a newspaper, and anything difficult or embarrassing to the Government is then explained away by commentators. With this sort of governmental control, where will freedom be?
Who asked for this legislation? We would like to know if the Minister would tell us. Did it have the same paternity as the truth squad? Did it have the same paternity as the campaign which has been waged across this country? I dislike mentioning myself personally, but it is a campaign designed to destroy, to assassinate. of measure could best be introduced in some other way.

I have some strange ideas-maybe they are not so strange-for someone who is a member of this party. My strange ideas relate to the profit motive in newspapers. A few years ago I saw Mr. Roy Thomson being interviewed on television by one of Canada's leading intellectuals who, I am sure thought he was going to make mincemeat of Mr. Thomson. The burden of his argument went like this, "Mr. Thomson, don't you think it is a terrible thing that Canadian newspapers should be run for profit instead of ideology?" I was quite impressed with Roy Thomson's reply with his argument that if you run a newspaper essentially for profit you tend to be guided by public intention, by the need for public acceptance, and that this tends to neutralize a newspaper. A newspaper run with this motive does not get on a high horse and start developing ideologies. This, I think, is a good thing.
I am far less suspicious of a newspaper that is run for profit than of a newspaper run to promote some ideology. All of us at some time or another would wish to see a newspaper that in its editorial policies favoured us quite strongly. But as Mr. Thomson pointed out, the day may come when it

However, that can be done on another occasion. But clause 19 does seem to introduce a principle-and this has been referred to by my hon. friend from Wellington South-which constitutes a travesty on the whole constitutional process by making use of the power of taxation as a means by which the British North America Act can be circumvented and the Federal Government can enter into spheres of jurisdiction and authority which
June 17. 1965

certainly do not lie within the contemplation of that Act.
As hon. Members know, section 91(3) of the B.N.A. Act says the Federal Government has jurisdiction with respect to "the raising of money by any method or system of taxation." Certainly any Member of the Opposition who by asking questions has made an effort to find out why this Government does the things it does from day to day, knows how difficult it is at any time to obtain a straight answer in respect of any matter, important or unimportant.
I should like to conclude my remarks by quoting the last paragraph of an editorial

which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 16, 1965, as follows:
No one, least of all the newspapers of Canada, quarrels with the government's objective of assuring a press which is completely controlled by Canadians and immune from foreign ownership. It is with the method Mr. Gordon has chosen that every responsible newspaper must strongly disagree and, if it is adopted by Parliament, seek to have rescinded by some future government.
I should like to say this. This is North America, not South America; this is a democracy with a democratic Government, not a dictatorship. We do not use the gag or the mailed fist to stop the newspapers from saying what they desire to say in their columns. If that is the intention of the Government, then I say once again: Smarten up; take this legislation off the order paper, and let us get on with the business of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a comment or two following the statement made by the hon. Member for Peace River with regard to the matter of a tax concession to farmers who clear land. We are all well aware of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture is concerned with a certain class of farmer who is in a fairly high economic bracket and does, I am sure, pay income tax. However, anyone who has really looked at agriculture in the development areas of northern Ontario or other areas of northern Canada where land clearance is still worth while, and an economic proposition from the point of view of the country would have to question whether or not this provision really gives much of a concession to such farmers.
It is quite true that in some areas of southern Ontario land is being cleared, and
1	am sure this is probably the case in the southern areas of other provinces as well. I know that considerable land clearance is going on in southern Quebec. But such clearance in the main is not being done by individual farmers setting out to homestead, as many of those in the newer areas are doing. Rather, it involves the clearing of land on a fairly large scale.
It is well understood that the Province of Ontario has been concerned about land clearance and I know that this is also true of the Province of Quebec. The former Federal Government showed seme inclination to interest itself in this field through ARDA. I think it is a fact that a great deal of land has been cleared in Ontario and Quebec that never should have been cleared at all. This has resulted in a very detrimental situation and
June 17, 1985

one that ARDA was really established to correct.
We know that the Ottawa valley, for instance, once had one of the largest and most valuable stands of timber in the country. The trees were cut down and land was cleared for agricultural purposes which any agency interested in the conservation of our resources would know should never have been cleared. As a result water and land conservation problems have arisen which we are now having to face, and under ARDA a program of planting trees is being carried out because of the fact that the land is not agricultural and never will be.
It is also known that much of the land being cleared in many areas today is being cleared with the help of provincial grants, which take care of about half of the actual cost of clearing the land. In northern Ontario, where land is selling for $30 to $50 an acre, it has always surprised me to find the Farm Credit Corporation, a Federal agency, making grants of from $12 to $18 an acre for clearing farmland, while the Ontario Provincial Government has paid $25 an acre for the clearing of similar land on the basis of a 50 per cent grant.
I am well aware that there are farmers in my area who will take advantage of this tax concession. I as a Member of Parliament can take advantage of it. I have been thinking for some time of clearing some land I own, and I am also often concerned about the amount of income tax we have to pay. I also know that I was going to be able to clear some of the land in another manner and that this provision obviously cuts me off now from doing so. The fact is that companies will want to get into the business of clearing land for purposes of speculation. They will have the equipment to do so and they will find that clearing land can be done for the grants that will be allowed, and they will also be entitled to a write-off for tax purposes.
I wish to refer to another point brought out very clearly by the hon. Member for Peace River who represents a large segment of the newly developed areas of Canada. I am not too sure whether the riding of Peace River covers what I consider to be the Peace River area, but I know of people who have gone to the Peace River area and have secured land there, just as people have in my riding. On the basis of cases that have come to my attention and my personal knowledge I know that most of these people have no income at all. In my area they can receive 22620-163
Income Tax Act
no assistance from the Provincial Government because they have less than 25 acres cleared and the agricultural representative considers that they do not earn half their income from the land they have cleared. These people, of course, are not now eligible for assistance from the province and they are not going to be eligible under the provision in the resolution, for the simple reason they are not earning any income and do not pay any income tax.
I am wondering whether some safeguard is going to be provided by the Department of Finance and whether the Minister is really going to consider certain things that may be in direct conflict with some of the other things the Government is doing. I have always been concerned with what appears to be the lack of knowledge of the Liberal Government with regard to the purpose for which the ARDA program was established. I think we have here another indication that there has not really been too much co-ordination of thinking between the people who are going to benefit from this provision, and those concerned with ARDA who really believe in the conservation of our natural resources and the application of those resources to bring about the greatest economic benefit to the Canadian people.
We know that many of the areas that are going to be reforested under the ARDA program are areas where the Ontario Government made a considerable monetary contribution for the clearing of the land without really knowing if the land should have been cleared. subtopic: REPORT RESULTING IN RETIREMENT OF R.C.M.P. OFFICERS
REPORT RESULTING IN RETIREMENT OF R.C.M.P. OFFICERS
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the report prepared by the Commissioner of the R.C.M. Police which resulted in the forced retirement of Chief Superintendent Belec and SubInspector Poitras.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have waited some time to have an opportunity to enlarge upon the request that 1 first made in the last session of Parliament to have tabled in the House the report that was prepared by the Commissioner of the R.C.M. Police for the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Favreau).
I realize that when the Government spokesman answers me he will no doubt explain to the House, through a long recital of precedents, the reason why this should not be done; but it is my intention in as brief a manner as possible to state the reasons why I feel this should be done, and should have been done many months ago.
The situation related to this matter is almost unprecedented for, to the best of my knowledge, what happened was that a request was made by the Commissioner of the R.C.M.P. to the Minister of Justice to dismiss the two individuals mentioned, Chief Superintendent Belec and Sub-Inspector Poitras. One will quickly appreciate that these were not insignificant individuals in the R.C.M.P. Indeed, it is my understanding that Chief Superintendent Belec was in charge of the R.C.M. Police in the Province of Quebec, and it is indeed a serious matter when the Commissioner of the R.C.M. Police considers it necessary to make a recommendation to the Minister of Justice to have an Order in Council passed for their dismissal.
One must always keep in mind that the high reputation of the R.C.M. Police must be maintained at all times, regardless of the involvement of any individual; but it is my belief that the Minister of Justice did not do that on this occasion. When he received this request from the Commissioner he had two alternatives available to him. Certainly we in the House do not expect the Minister to rubber-stamp anything that might come before him from the Commissioner, but at the same time we do expect that, when a request comes to his desk from the Commissioner,
Motions for Papers
he will give it that consideration whifch warrants action almost immediately.
[DOT] (6:10 pjn.)
In the circumstances the Minister had two alternatives available to him. He could have said to the Commissioner: The facts as set out are correct; the action you recommend is correct, and an order in council will be prepared immediately for the dismissal of these men. Or he could have said: The facts are not serious enough to warrant the kind of action you recommend. In either case the Commissioner and the R.C.M.P. would have known where they stood. But the Minister of Justice, instead, did the worst thing possible: He did nothing. He allowed the matter to hang in the air in suspended animation. He allowed it to hang there for months, and during that period of time a great deal of talk developed which materially affected morale in the force. He allowed two senior men, men who had spent many years in the R.C.M.P., to remain on tenterhooks not knowing what their fate would be. The Minister placed the force in a most demoralizing position for reasons no one knows-reasons which no one can know unless the report in question is tabled in this House, or a public inquiry is recommended by the Government.
In the end, what we find is that the two individuals involved are no longer members of the R.C.M.P. But they do have their pensions. It is something very strange when two individuals find themselves in a position where they can no longer remain members of this illustrious organization-their actions have resulted in their no longer being considered capable of remaining in the force-while at the same time they are allowed to leave with their pensions.
Mr. Speaker, one is either guilty or not guilty. If these men were not guilty of the offences of which they were accused, they should have been allowed to return to the posts from which they had been suspended. If they were, they should be dismissed, brought before the courts and prosecuted for the offences which are alleged. We find it is impossible to learn exactly what transpired except that these men are no longer members of the R.C.M.P. and that they have obtained their pension entitlement from that force. With the affairs which have taken place in the Province of Quebec over the past two years and with the involvement of Members of the Liberal party in so many of these scandals, and with the involvement of those officers in matters associated with suggested devious ac-

June 17, 1965
Motions for Papers
tions, one begins to wonder whether the Government is not afraid of what might be said by these two individuals if a public inquiry were announced and those involved were allowed to state their case and place their story before the Canadian people.
I am responsible enough to know that one does not in ordinary circumstances expect the Government to agree to the tabling of a report of this kind. But these are not ordinary circumstances: These are very strange circumstances. These are circumstances of the kind which revolve around everything which has been going on between this Government, the upper echelon of the executive which serves the Cabinet of this country, and organized criminals in the Province of Quebec. If these men have been involved in any way, it is my belief the Canadian people should know about it. They should know also that the Commissioner was willing to take action of the kind which would eliminate this kind of thing from the R.C.M.P. Instead, we find the Minister of Justice and the Government unwilling to provide the facts for the Canadian people, though willing to allow the reputation of the R.C.M.P. to be discredited for their own protection.
I believe that in fairness to everyone concerned this report should be made available or a public inquiry should be set up in order that the Canadian people may be allowed to judge the facts in a public way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORT RESULTING IN RETIREMENT OF R.C.M.P. OFFICERS
speechtext:
I am just dealing with the rather contemptible remarks of your colleague. I make no insinuations. I say directly that they are contemptible.
The hon. Member has professed some familiarity with the precedents and the law affecting this situation. He says he is aware of the long established principles which have been laid down in this House in connection with matters of this kind. Yet he makes the statement-a puzzling one in view of the clear provisions of the R.C.M.P. Act-that either these persons are guilty or they are not. He says that if they are guilty they should be dismissed and brought before the courts.
0	(6:20 p.m.)
I think it is necessary for the benefit of the hon. Member and for the sake of the record to make clear exactly what are the provisions of the R.C.M.P. Act in this respect, and the purpose of those sections which provide for disciplinary procedure-the procedure followed in this case. Before doing so
1	would just like to make reference to some of the precedents in this House which make it quite clear that it is long established tradition that the internal documents of the R.C.M. Police relating to disciplinary matters should not be made subject to an order under this type of motion. The rule, of course, is founded very soundly on principle and is related to the special character of the service which the R.C.M. Police perform on behalf of Canada. It is related to the very high standards of discipline which in part at least have contributed to the high reputation that force has, and to its very great responsibility as a police force, which is something all police forces have.
I would like to make reference to Hansard for May 7, 1952, and to a motion by the hon. Member for Prince Albert, now the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), for the disclosure of all the evidence taken on a similar kind of disciplinary proceeding against a former member of the R.C.M.P. Speaking on behalf of the government of that time, the former Minister of Justice, Hon. Stuart S. Garson, laid out several principles which I think it is well for the House to bear in mind in dealing with this particular motion. After making reference to the fact that there were precedents-and he cited them on that date-for the non-production of this kind of material, he went on as follows:
The right of the Commissioner, acting under the authority given to him by the Act and under the
June 17, 1965



general supervision of the Minister, to engage and discharge personnel at his discretion has over the years proved to be one of the principal factors in maintaining a high level of discipline and efficiency within the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Any suggestion that that authority may be questioned would weaken the whole fabric of discipline and control.
Then he continues in the same passage:
The strict, even severe, standards of discipline insisted upon by the force are well known and are accepted by recruits when they are engaged as well as by older members each time they re-engage. The reputation the force enjoys and is striving successfully to maintain in the face of recent substantial expansion is based very largely on adherence to these standards.
That particular motion was refused by the House. It was submitted to a vote of the House and the vote was negative. One would have assumed that if the hon. Member for Prince Albert, who was the mover of the motion at that time, had felt the proceedings with regard to disciplinary action in the R.C.M. Police were wrongful, if he had felt there should have been a change in the governing statutes so as to make these proceedings public, he would have taken action to bring about that change. The fact is that while the right hon. gentleman headed the Government of this country the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act was brought before the House, and perhaps even the hon. Member for Cumberland was present when it was submitted to some very searching scrutiny by the Opposition of that day.
It might be useful, Mr. Speaker, to put on the record the exact details of both the disciplinary proceedings which are followed and some of the statements made by the former Minister of Justice, Hon. E. D. Fulton, on the question of disciplinary proceedings and what were the views of that Government. Under Section 25 of the Statute there is set out a series of offences which are referred to as major disciplinary offences for which disciplinary action may be taken against members of the force, and under Section 26 distinction is made between those offences and certain other violations of the regulations which are referred to as minor service offences.
Hon. Members will recognize at once that Section 25, and indeed the regulations, impose higher standards in many cases than are expected of a person in normal employment. The disciplinary offences are put there in order to maintain the particularly high standard of performance and service in this police force, and because someone may have been tried under that particular section, as
Motions for Papers
was the case with the two former officers involved in this motion, it does not necessarily indicate that there has been anything in the nature of an offence against the Criminal Code nor does it necessarily indicate, as the hon. Member seemed to think, that the individuals in question should be tried in the courts or prosecuted in the courts for these offences. This force, like the armed services, is a highly disciplined one and the failure to observe these particularly high standards may result in this disciplinary action being taken, which of course would not necessarily involve and did not in this case involve the bringing of any proceedings in the criminal courts against the members.
Once an offence has been discovered it is provided by section 32 of the Statute that an investigation is to be carried out, and if after the investigation it appears to an officer that a member has committed a major service offence, a report shall be made to the Commissioner, and if the Commissioner feels the evidence justifies it he shall direct that a written charge be prepared and served on the member. The Statute goes on, under Section 34, to provide the procedural rules which are to be followed in trials under this provision.
This proceeding under the former Statute and as contained in the present one is not a proceeding in the normal course, and it is because of the special character of the R.C.M. Police that the former Government supported by the hon. gentleman decided to take this particular matter outside the ordinary courts and establish it in a particular tribunal to be conducted internally by the R.C.M. Police. Under these provisions, once the sentence is given, by Section 35 it is provided that if the presiding officer is satisfied on the evidence submitted at the trial that the accused is guilty of the offence as charged, he must so find and the presiding officer may then sentence the accused to such punishment as is provided by that part of the Statute.

Mr. Speaker, as an ex-member of the Royal Canadian Mounted 'Police and having some intimate knowledge of this matter, I think I might be permitted to say a word. In my opinion the Parliamentary Secretary is setting up a straw man in imputing motives to the hon. Member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates). I am convinced that the hon. Member for Cumberland wants nothing more than complete frankness. I am not going to support the demand for the production of these papers, without some reservations, but I certainly feel that the matter has to be cleared up.
The Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is in a very unenviable position. On the one hand, he is permitted to exercise almost unlimited discretion and in certain cases the Government is willing to stake its reputation and its whole future on his judgment. On the other hand, other decisions made by the same man are either completely ignored or overridden. I suggest that you cannot have it both ways. If the Commissioner of the Mounted Police is so omniscient that he knows all the answers and his decisions are to be accepted without reference to a higher authority, that is fine; but let that be the system. I believe that generally speaking no person in Canada should be seized with the responsibility of making irrevocable decisions. The House of Commons is the only tribunal which should make irrevocable decisions, and even here our decisions are not really irrevocable because they are subject to the opinions of the Canadian people by the changing of governments.
I think this whole matter should be brought out in the open with complete frankness. It is common gossip not only among the people of Canada but among members of the force itself that there are aspects of this case which have not been brought to the attention of the Canadian people, or even of Parliament. It is very unfortunate that this situation arose because the fact is that any suspicion of protection or the exercise of unfair ministerial discretion certainly reflects on the ability of

the Mounted Police to run their own operation. There is a reflection on the Minister himself if he refuses to give frank answers to the House.
The matter is so serious that I should like the Minister himself to explain why he used his ministerial discretion. I do not deny him that discretion, but over the head of the Mounted Police I think there must be either an independent police commission, something in which I do not believe, or an alert Parliament; and in my view an alert Parliament is all the ombudsman we need. When proper questions are asked in the House I think we are entitled to frank answers. I for one do not impute low intentions to hon. members opposite and I certainly fly to the rescue of Members on this side when all we are seeking is common justice.
From time to time the Mounted Police are forced to discipline members of that organization. I ought to know because I was released from my duties in that force some 20-odd years ago for the crime of getting married without permission. The rule with regard to marriage was changed from six years to seven years service without consulting me, but in spite of that fact I saw fit to get married, which I think is the right of every Canadian citizen over the age of 21, and I was dismissed and fined. I have not complained and I am not complaining now. The standards of the Mounted Police require absolute conformity to the regulations and in my opinion this should apply from the latest joined constable up to the Commissioner himself.
I am not entitled to a full pension. My pension was reduced by 33J per cent some 25 years ago for the crime of getting married and it is still reduced by that amount. I have no recourse, but I am not complaining. I am merely stating the facts of the case. I should like to know whether the far seeing Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) would like to review my case some day and decide quite impartially and fairly whether I should not be treated in the same way as these two gentlemen who were relieved of their duties, or asked to retire, or whatever it was that happened to them. We do not know. However, I venture to guess that their pensions have not been reduced. I will also venture to say that they are allowed to wear what is known as the long distance medal. I am not allowed to wear that medal, although my combined service in the Mounted Police and Her Majesty's forces amounts to over 23 years. My service has been smeared because I had

the temerity to get married. These men have been charged with embezzlement and misappropriation of funds. That is the only knowledge we have because the facts have not been made public. Must we sit here quietly and trust to ministerial discretion in this regard without explanations and answers to perfectly legitimate questions in the House?
This is not the first time I have mentioned this subject in the House. I have spoken about it on more than one occasion. We hear these days about angry young men. At times I think I am becoming a very angry middle aged man. There is no reason we should not receive answers to questions which are put in good faith. If our questions are not going to be answered in good faith, I am afraid we are going to have to replace those who sit on the treasury benches by people who will answer in good faith. It is not good enough for the Government to say that the former Government did not do it and therefore they are not going to. Surely that is not a good excuse for a Government that knows all the answers.
