Again it seems to me we bog each other down in these points of order. We have come here to discuss the business of the nation and I am going to try to keep myself on that tack.
I agree with some of these improvements, including the so-called 10 per cent reduction in personal income tax, but had the Minister lowered the basic exemption it would have been much preferable. The whole purpose of income tax, as I understand it, is to seek

June 17, 1965
Income Tax Act
the big pocket, and to make it possible for those who do not have enough money to live by the contributions of those who do. If this is our avowed intention, then the proper thing to do is make sure we have a basic living before dipping into it for extraordinary expenditure, and it is only an extraordinary expenditure which should make it necessary for people to dip into their basic living to pay for things which other people need. This may sound a little socialistic, but I call it co-operative living.
With inflation I suggest that anything less than a $3,000 exemption for married couples would not be sensible. I am against moonlighting, but some people say it is perfectly all right if you cannot live on $2,500 a year to get $5,000 by putting your wife out to work. Surely that is not the avowed intention of the Government.
I am pleased with the provision covering improvement of land, but I agree with the hon. Member for Timiskaming that it is an empty gesture toward people living on homesteads, people in the Peace River and Athabasca districts and the outlying northern districts, because the person clearing land there has no income during the time he is doing it.
There should be exemptions for land clearing if a man is clearing land to make himself a better farm and a more productive unit, and I suggest there should be an income tax reduction for the digging of wells, the damming of streams and such things, especially for reforestation as a result of land clearing. I know thousands of acres of land, principally sand hills, where it would be better for people to put it back into evergreens and fast growing wood rather than clear it for farming. Therefore I think the Minister should get together with ARDA people and the farm union people, rather than stepping off in the blind and just making tax reduction gestures. With the proper help farmers can make themselves better farms and preserve the natural resources of the country.
It is probably fair to allow union dues as tax exemptions. It is impossible for many skilled trades people to make a living unless they contribute to a union, and if federal and provincial statutes make it necessary or advisable for people to belong to a union in order to make a living union dues should be income tax free. However, I think we should attach a rider and say when these dues go to the financing of political parties, and are used for political purposes by unions, they should not

be tax free. I can see no reason why a good Tory or Liberal should not have his contributions to party funds exempted from income tax, if no such rider is attached to union due exemptions. Unless union dues go into welfare funds or are used for the protection of unemployed workers, they should not be totally exempted from tax.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
The paragraph which worries me most, and which has been debated at length this afternoon, is the one concerning freedom of the press. The Minister has said that when this becomes law it will not be abused, and that we are putting up straw men. I say they are putting a tiger's teeth into the head of a sheep. Although the sheep may bleat comfortably and quietly in the fold, how do we know that it may not become a tiger? I would be horrified to think I had helped to pass a statute which put teeth into a provision by which I might myself be torn asunder. Perhaps it makes an amusing picture-someone with democratic ideas fleeing over the hill with an important part of his trousers missing, and the tiger licking his chops.
This is one of the package deals I am supposed to accept because I am in favour of tax exemptions in respect to land clearance, or parts of the ARDA program. Unless we divide this resolution clause by clause I may well find myself, in helping to give the homesteader who digs a well an income tax rebate, voting to restrict the freedom of the press. We accept the freedom of the press in this country without much question. It is our way of life and I suppose we do not think about defending it any more. That is when the thief always comes-when you are asleep. If the Minister is as innocent as he says he is, it is our plain duty to shake him, wake him up and tell him what is in this package deal he is asking us to pass. This resolution reminds me of one of those iced cakes I was speaking about a few days ago, those iced cakes which are full of bitter sawdust. I would not be surprised to find, in view of the Minister's record, that he really is innocent and naive. He offers us these cakes and he does not even know the icing is thin and the sawdust unpalatable. On other occasions when he has been told about this he has withdrawn, and put a few raisins in there. I beg him to take another look at this resolution and see whether he can take these sour nuts out of the cake and give us those parts which are acceptable to the economy.
June 17, 1965

Let him not lay the blame on the O'Leary report. The O'Leary report nowhere suggested that pressure should he placed on the press of Canada. Quite the contrary; the report was intended to put up one more peg on which freedom might hang, not to provide rope on which to hang freedom, in the other sense. This Government is too fond of blaming its failures on other individuals or organizations or commissions. If you are looking for weak arguments to back up this type of legislation, somebody may have been reading the gospel according to Kent and Lamontagne. This is the kind of two-headed axe with which they intend to chop down the tree of freedom. This may sound like a florid remark but I do not know how you can expect a man to sit quietly here in the Committee when the press itself is allergic to this proposal, and such notable Whig newspapers as the Winnipeg Free Press have openly called the Minister of Finance a prevaricator. We are not allowed to do that in this Chamber, but I am tempted to agree with this florid opinion from that Whig newspaper. It is only open criticism of the Government, apparently, which can bring them to their senses. We are not allowed, under the changed rules, to do it in the House so there is all the more reason why we need a free press to do it.
In recent years I have at times thought Canada was sound asleep-that the people did not listen to what we said, either here in the House or outside it. I began to think the press was only interested in florid stories and would print nothing unless a man criticized his boss or left his party, or something like that. Perhaps it is because this is closer to home that we have heard so much about it. It would be strange if the press of Canada did not come to the rescue of the press of Canada. In this regard I support the views the press has taken. I do not care whether they appear in a Tory paper or a Whig paper or a red paper. The truth is just as valuable, regardless of the editorial policy. I intend to write to the Free Press in Winnipeg and say: Bravo! This is a fresh breath of air coming out of Western Canada at a time when it is badly needed.
I do not usually quote poetry. I do not think this is very a poetic situation. But about 100 years ago Alfred Lord Tennyson in England summed it up very well. He was answering a hypothetical question-why he stayed in the foggy old island and put up with the English class system, vested interincome Tax Act
ests and so forth. And he gave the answer in four lines of poetry which have always stuck in my mind. The last two are the punch lines:
It is a land where girt with friends or foes
A man may speak the thing he will.
Believe me, if we ever reach the point in Canada where any Government or group of people could control the press of this country you will find me living in the hills, and I will be a very unpleasant customer. As long as a free Parliament stands, I know this: The main peg on which our freedom hangs is freedom of the press. We are going to have it as long as free men live in this country or we shall know the reason why. It is going to take more than a rule book to stop us. If ever there was a filibuster required it should be required until this clause of this particular resolution is taken right out, like a rotten nut out of the same sawdust cake. Then we will not be forced to vote for something we do not like merely because it is wrapped up among certain things we do like.

I wish to speak first of all on the part of this resolution which has to do with agriculture, and I should like to compliment the Minister for having incorporated in these provisions some relief for farmers in respect of two particularly vexing expenditures with which they are often faced, namely, clearing land and laying tile drainage.
It is true that in areas where there is a tremendous amount of work to be done and whole farms have to be cleared there could easily be no income at all for taxation purposes and the clause would not be applicable.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
But there are, on the other hand, as is the case in the area that I have the honour to represent, many farms that are covered with small wooded areas varying from 5 to 50 acres, many farms which have pastures which for one reason or another have become overgrown with thorn bushes and are not as productive as they might be. I am sure that this particular measure which exempts expenses incurred in clearing this type of land will be especially beneficial to our farmers. In our area a tremendous amount of land is not drained, and farmers are going to be very pleased indeed to find that their representations over the years in this particular field have at last met with success, and the Minister is granting them this much needed

June 17, 1965
Income Tax Act
income tax exemption in connection with expenses incurred in laying tile drainage.
I am particularly impressed with subparagraph (b) which deals with the exemption from income tax of expenses incurred for landscaping property used by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income. I hope that the interpretation of this measure will mean that this relief will be available to farmers across our country, because for many years the lack of income or the time of those working the farm has made it impossible to care for lawns and plant the various bushes which are so necessary to make these farms the perfect picture that they might become. If this provision is interpreted in such a way that exempts expenses incurred in landscaping this type of property, I am sure many farms will benefit from it.
Under subparagraph (d) one can deduct from income tax expenses incurred on account of the cost of making representations to a government, municipality or other public authority in connection with a business carried on by the taxpayer, including representations for the purpose of obtaining a licence, permit, franchise or trade-mark. I hope this particular provision will be interpreted in such a way that farmers and businessmen will be able to claim exemption from income tax of any expenses incurred in making representations to government in regard to charges and assessments levied against them. There have been many instances where charges or assessments that have been made against farmers and small businessmen have not been valid. In some instances large expenditures would have been incurred in making these representations and it has been found impossible to make the necessary recommendations. These costs should be allowed to be written off as expenses incurred in the business operation.
Having dealt with that matter, Mr. Chairman, I, too, must turn to paragraph 19, because I think in its present form and the manner in which it has been introduced, it is a deliberate affront to every Member who conscientiously represents Canadians in this House of Commons. After listening to the various speakers who have preceded me it has become increasingly apparent that the smokescreens are rolling away from the course of action taken by the present Government. The various policies and the way in which they have been introduced during the session have made it abundantly clear how the Gov-

ernment proposes to deal with controversial legislation. Mr. Chairman, I listened to the Minister of Finance when he explained patiently to the House of Commons that no government would even conceive of the idea of applying any sort of pressure or control on the news media of this country, even if this particular resolution were adopted. I also heard this Minister explain patiently to the House that our publishers have been consulted and there was no indication of any opposition from those directly concerned with this particular provision. But you can understand, Mr. Chairman, my concern about the credibility of this Minister when, like every other Member of the House, I receive telephone calls and there come across my desk representations in the form of telegrams and correspondence stating in no uncertain terms the strongest opposition to this particular provision.
This seems to be a pattern that is being adopted by the present Government. Here we have a whole series of measures in which is incorporated what we feel to be relief to the people who need income tax relief. We have relief for farmers, for businessmen and for labour. In some instances this relief is very minute, but it is at least a start. Then we have incorporated in paragraph 19 a principle which it is almost impossible to accept, knowing the way this Government campaigns on the election platform. Everyone sitting in the Opposition knows that if we vote against these measures on the basis that we are strongly opposed to controlling the press or limiting the freedom of the press in any way, we would be charged on the hustings with voting against exemptions of income tax and exemptions for expenses for land clearing, tile drainage, union dues and the whole gamut of those things contained in these resolutions. We would be subject to this type of attack on the hustings if we dared to oppose paragraph 19 in no uncertain terms.
I resent most vigorously another picture that is developing, and it is this. We are all concerned about a summer recess. We did not have one last year. We want to get back to our own constituencies; we want to be with our families.
Hear, hear.

But the same pattern is developing as developed last year. We are told, "Pass this legislation, or else". We are told that the Government stands or falls on certain legislation. We are told that if we do
June 17, 1965

not pass this legislation there will be no recess and we will be here all summer. Here we walk between the club and the carrot and are asked to take our choice. This is the kind of action on the part of this Government that I absolutely resent, and I know that every man in the Opposition resents it. We resent the attitude of a government that would not separate this resolution, which they know is contentious in some parts, and let us deal with it in that way, without having to determine how we are going to vote in connection with the whole package because we do not in any way agree with paragraph 19.
This is what has happened time and time again. They take an issue that has public favour and tie it in with something they know the Opposition find very difficult to tolerate. The same pattern is involved here as was involved in the reform of Parliament. What happened? This Government brought in desirable reforms of Parliament which all parties accepted, and then they buried in them the guillotine rule, which gives them control because they can stop our debating in the House. Now they are speaking of control of the press. They hold up their hands in holy horror when we suggest they are trying to control all the segments of this country. When we suggest they might be exercising some control over the C.B.C. we hear them deny this in the most vigorous way. But we have only to look back to see what happened to that great production of the Prime Minister that was made for the C.B.C. We know it is gathering dust somewhere, but we do not know where. Hon. gentlemen say they do not control the C.B.C.; yet the C.B.C. produces the film but could not put it over the air.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Then there is the Canada Pension Plan, which has now been adopted. We received warnings from financial circles that through the Canada Pension Plan governments, be they federal or provincial, or their appointees, could control the tremendous amounts of money brought into the plan, thus giving this Government a great deal of control over all finances in the country. So we have control of the C.B.C., control over finances, and we now see an attempt to control the press.
When is this type of action going to cease, Mr. Chairman? Perhaps now is the time for the Opposition to take a stand and say: No further. The people of Canada expect to have a democracy; they want a democracy. But the actions of this group opposite lead one to think that we are now heading toward a
Income Tax Act
dictatorship. We in the Opposition had been afraid that we were drifting toward a republic. It now begins to appear that we are drifting toward a dictatorship. We must watch what the Government is doing and the actions it is taking. We cannot accept paragraph 19 in its present form and I think the Government knows it. The Minister of Finance has been criticized over and over again for this type of action. The Government as a whole must take the responsibility for such action, not just the Minister of Finance.
I am hoping that the Government will seriously consider the suggestion which was put forward this afternoon by our leader, when he requested that this resolution be withdrawn. In this event we could then proceed into ways and means and deal with these matters in a responsible manner, this particular paragraph having been excluded. I suggest this paragraph was put in deliberately so as to force the Opposition into accepting it along with the other items included with it, thus placing responsibility on our shoulders. This is a deliberate plan to incorporate this disagreeable type of legislation in a honey-coated package, in the hope that the Opposition, either browbeaten or cajoled, will accept it in total.
Paragraph 19 will, I believe, in no way solve the problem to which it is directed but will put the Government in a position where it holds a sword over the heads of the entire press of the nation. But we are not only concerned with the press of this country; we are also concerned with the international press and about the entire picture which actions of this type can conjure up. And we have no guarantee that this is the end. We lost our vacation last year because we found dollar items buried in the estimates. This package deal is the same type of proceeding.
We in the Opposition are tired of these package deals. We think that the Government should stand on their own responsibility and introduce their measures into this Parliament in the way a responsible Canadian Government should, giving the Opposition an opportunity either to support or to vote against them, and to do so conscientiously without being blackmailed in the manner we are here, through the addition of the other items tied into this resolution. I, like all Members of the Opposition, believe that now is the time for the Government, if they are ever going to act like a responsible Canadian Government, to start acting like one and to withdraw this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to trespass too long on the time of the committee, but I should very much like to make a modest proposal to the Minister of Finance which I am sure he will find reasonable and which will not demand the expenditure of any funds by the Government. However, I would gladly yield my time to him if he would get up and say that he will separate this resolution and make it easier for Members to vote on it paragraph by paragraph, so we can approve those paragraphs we like and vote against those we cannot accept. Surely that makes good sense. It is a businesslike approach and is a way of delineating a complex resolution which cannot find, and certainly will not find, the total acceptance of this House. I know the Minister could do this, and if he really wants to curtail further debate on this resolution that is all that needs to be done. He need only offer to split the resolution into parts or to withdraw paragraph 19 of it.
If I may come to the modest proposal to which I referred, it deals with aid to agriculture which has really been left out of the particular paragraph of the resolution, but which was nevertheless referred to in the budget speech on April 26. The hon. Member for Victoria-Carleton and the hon. Member for Acadia have already referred to the fact that included in the budget is exemption of income tax on money expended on grain storage bins, yet in the resolution we find no reference to it. This is a grave and serious omission in view of the fact that the agricultural industry needs continuing attention. I am pleased to say that it had all kinds of attention from the previous Government, but the present Government seems to be devoid of new plans to aid this important industry.
My supposition-I think it is correct-is that silos, for example, which are used in the developing mechanization of dairy farms to feed dairy cattle, are still subject to a 20 per cent duty when imported from the United States. At the same time farm machinery is exempt from tax. This seems to me to be a contradiction. Both are tools needed in the dairy industry, yet there is a 20 per cent duty on silos and no tax at all on farm machinery.
The suggestion I made in writing to the Minister some days ago was in support of a resolution passed by the Interlake Regional Development Board of Manitoba, which has said that exemptions of capital investment in farm buildings should be applied to all farm structures, not just grain storage bins. I think
IMr. Danforth.]
this would be a tremendous incentive to improve what the Minister of Agriculture has referred to in various speeches across the country as rural slums. He has said that there is a great need to improve farm buildings across the country; and one way of giving an incentive to Canadian farmers, at the same time not costing the Government one penny, would be to make this incentive applicable to the whole structure of farming and to exempt capital cost or depreciation on farm buildings.
The policy of our tax structure these days is getting more and more to be one of penalizing the progressive. We can improve conditions, not just of farms, if we provide the kind of incentive of which I speak.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
In discussing the whole question of silos and grain storage there is a very remarkable difference between the taxation experience of our farmers, and that of farmers in the United States. In regard to silos again, since I want to make my point in this way, United States farmers have the benefit of a capital allowance plan whereby the cost of farm buildings can be depreciated in four years. In other words, they are allowed a depreciation of 25 per cent per year. Our farmers are allowed a 2 J per cent per year depreciation allowance, or capital cost allowance, so that it takes them 40 years to write off the cost of buildings which probably become useless to the farm operation in 10 or 15 years. In fairness to these farmers I think that this injustice should be corrected.
Another feature of the tax laws in the United States which appeals to me, is that feature which allows companies to build storage bins and silos and charge a rental for seven years, at the end of which time they sell them to the farmer for $1. This feature does away with capital cost allowances and depreciation.
That illustration clearly indicates that we in Canada are behind in our methods of providing incentives to the development of better and improved farms. I make the plea to the Government to remove entirely the duty on silos, and to change the capital cost allowance or depreciation rate on farm buildings from 2J per cent per year to 25 per cent per year, allowing farm buildings to be written off in a four year period.
When I commenced my remarks I suggested that the proposals I intended to make were moderate and would not cost the Treasury any money at all, but would provide marvellous
June 17, 1965

incentives to our farmers, so that perhaps by the Centennial year the rural scenery in this country would be vastly improved. I could perhaps have followed up the excellent comments made by various other Members of the Opposition parties in respect of other paragraphs of the resolution but, as I intended, I have confined my remarks to those two subjects I have mentioned. I draw these remarks sincerely to the attention of the Minister, and I hope he will give them some serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, while I must certainly subscribe to the views of the two speakers who preceded me in regard to the evil practices of governments presenting us with package deals, I must say that I am always impressed by the ability of parties in opposition to peer past the mote in their own eye to see the beam in the Government's eye, when the Government follows the same practice that they followed when they were in office. I suggest this is merely an example of that which Acton suggested: All power corrupts. We can be thankful that this is a minority Government in view of the fact the Minister of Finance is not likely to obtain absolute power and thereby become absolutely corrupt.
One of the favourite parlour games of Members of the Opposition, particularly in this Parliament, is to examine all the possible fluctuating fortunes of Members of the Privy Council on the other side within the framework of the Liberal Party, and what position of any Member of the Privy Council excites more interest than that of the Minister of Finance? The question of the day very often is: Is Walter up or is he down? Speaking personally, I may say I am always rather cheered when I see evidence that perhaps he is up, and I feel a little depressed when I see evidence that perhaps he is down. I would not want anyone to think that this means too much more than that he is the best of a bad lot.
I am impelled to speak tonight, Mr. Chairman, because of a remark the Minister made when my colleague, the hon. Member for Port Arthur, introduced an amendment to the notorious paragraph 19(a) of this resolution. At that time you will recall that the Minister said he had great sympathy for the purpose behind that amendment. This is interesting to me because I had come to the conclusion that, since the Minister had seen fit to make a special exception of two periodicals, he is a secret Time magazine addict,

or is accustomed to taking Reader's Digest to bed with him in order to gain the benefit of the ersatz culture of that magazine, which I find rather a despondent situation. His comment implies that he has great sympathy with the idea that this should not have been done, and we are forced to ask ourselves why it was done when this responsible Minister apparently felt unable to bring such a resolution before the House, and that he had to make this special exception for Time magazine and Reader's Digest. If this was not done because he has some love for those periodicals, there must be some other reason. 1 can only suppose that, unlike Jacob wrestling with the Angels of the Lord, the Minister of Finance wrestled and was thrown by some emissaries of the devil, who insisted that the two magazines should be subsidized by the taxpayers of Canada to further debase the intellectual standards of the people of Canada.
I wonder whether, in view of that evidence that the Minister lost out in this action, he wanted to do a worthy act but was not allowed to do it; because he has told us he has sympathy for the purposes of the amendment, but by his actions has indicated that he was unable to produce any concrete action to carry his sympathy into fact. I suppose we will now be told that he is planning, as he has told us he was going to plan, some other way of curbing these two rather pernicious periodicals.
On April 26 of this year as recorded at page 435 of Hansard the Minister said this, in the course of his budget speech to the House:
-nor will advertising in the two small foreign-owned weekly newspapers already being published in this country. The question of the subsidized postal rates now enjoyed by the Canadian editions of non-Canadian periodicals will be studied as part of a general review being made of postal rates.
I presume part of that general review will also entail a very careful redefinition of what constitutes a Canadian publication. Had it not been for the fact that the Minister has by his actions admitted that he was unable to persuade his colleagues to withdraw the subsidy for Time and Reader's Digest, one might be quite hopeful that he was actually going to do something about the postal rates now enjoyed by those two foreign publications.
[DOT] (7:50 pun.)
We have to consider two things. Has the Minister any assurance to give us that he is going to prevail over the forces of evil among his colleagues and solve this problem, which

he was not allowed to do in the obvious way of doing it, or has this been merely a little carrot he was holding before us, suggesting that if we pass the iniquitous paragraph 19(a) he would try to do by the back door what he was not allowed to do by the front door? It seems to me we need some assurances from him that these words of his on April 26 had some meaning and were not just a meaningless gesture toward the recriminations he was likely to receive when the House realized that once again the Government of Canada was not prepared to deal with these two publications. It is a fact that this Government is not any more courageous than its predecessor in office, which contented itself by appointing a Royal Commission and letting the matter drop. Nothing was done as a result of that Royal Commission and Senator O'Leary's work went up the chimney. This present Government is in no better shape. I think that the night before last the Minister, perhaps having been somewhat irritated by the remarks of my colleague, the hon. Member for Port Arthur, may have gone a little further than he would have done otherwise when, rather like a rooster on a dung-heap, he jumped and flapped his wings and said that the Government would stand or fall on the position of Time and Reader's Digest. It seems an astonishing thing to me for the Government of Canada to be prepared to stand or fall on the maintenance of the position of these two disreputable periodicals. It seems an astonishing thing that the Government, in the words of the Minister, is prepared to stake its life in order to provide special favours at the expense of the taxpayers to support these two extremely deplorable publications which we can well do without in Canada and which at least we should not subsidize to the detriment of Canadian periodicals, Canadian identity and Canadian public life as we are doing today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will be glad to make a very short statement, Mr. Chairman. I do not think there is anything in particular in this resolution to which I need to draw the attention of hon. Members of the Committee. It does provide for certain relief in the case of British exporters. As my hon. friend knows, the British have felt for some time that they have been under a disadvantage in their efforts to export to Canada. I was in London in July of 1964 and on that occasion I said that we would look into the matter and if we felt they were justified in their complaints I would suggest certain changes at the time of the budget.
We did review this matter and we felt, particularly in view of the difficulties that the British have been having lately, that some changes should be made in the administration of the Act. If it meets with the approval of the Committee, I should like to call on my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, who administers the Act, to continue the explanation.

Mr. Chairman, during his budget speech on April 26 my colleague, the Minister of Finance, announced several proposed changes in the Customs Act. Two
Customs Act
of the proposals deal with matters raised by the Auditor General relating to practices followed by the Department of National Revenue in releasing goods under bond and in assessing duties and taxes on foreign Government owned surplus goods disposed of in Canada. The proposed changes will implement the recommendations made in this connection by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.
The third proposal deals with the discriminatory effect which the valuation provisions of the Customs Act have on certain compact countries, which matter has been brought to our attention by the British. The fourth point relates to a situation which is regarded by Canadian manufacturers as a loophole in the law in that in certain circumstances foreign exporters are able to avail themselves of lower values for duty than would normally be the case simply by altering the route of shipment to Canada. The proposed change will remedy this situation. The fifth change which is proposed in the Customs Act is a consequential one in numbering resulting from the introduction of the new section which I have just described.

Mr. Chairman, in examining the various paragraphs of the resolution to amend the Customs Act perhaps I might be permitted in my general remarks to comment on each paragraph as I go along. There may be other Members of the Opposition who will then wish to comment on individual paragraphs. I should like to make a suggestion, Mr. Chairman, to avoid the confusion in discussion which arose on the last resolution. After the Minister and one representative from each of the parties have had a general go at the resolution I suggest that the discussion be limited to the paragraphs seriatim. I think this will create some continuity of discussion.
I trust I have made my point clear, Mr. Chairman. With regard to the nature of our discussion I suggest that after a ministerial statement and a general statement by a spokesman for each party the discussion should then be limited to each paragraph seriatim in order to avoid the going forward and then coming back in which we engaged during our discussion of the last resolution. I think this will make for better continuity in our discussion.
We have no objection.

That is standard procedure. So far as paragraph 1 is concerned, its pur-

June 17, 1965
Customs Act
pose is to provide what one might term administrative ease for the benefit of both the Government and the importer. I do not think it causes any undue difficulty and it is related to paragraph 7 which is consequential upon paragraph 1.
However, when I come to paragraph 2, which adds a subsection to section 22, I am reminded of a certain debate that took place in 1961 when the Government of the day proposed to introduce ministerial discretion with regard to the Customs Tariff Act. At that time there was a great holler and to-do from those then on this side of the House. I can remember the Minister of Transport, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the President of the Privy Council, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, crying to high heaven for days that the proposed action was arbitrary, that here was another case of ministerial discretion. They did so even though the late Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, then Minister of National Revenue, indicated that under the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff Act there were only 60 instances where the Minister was given discretion. I find this proposal passing strange in view of the fact that members of the present administration objected, objected and objected again when they were in the Opposition at that time. If ever there was an opportunity or, shall we say, an encouragement to apply the guillotine, it was on that occasion. Every possible step in the rule book was used to try and block the legislation in the House, and then of course it was blocked in the Senate.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Personally I think the Opposition may have had something on that occasion, but a position had been taken that there had to be the exercise of ministerial discretion in class or kind, without appeal. From an administrative point of view that was absolutely right, but from a public point of view there were objections. When we come to paragraph 5 of the resolution I am going to indicate to hon. Members that here we have an introduction of ministerial discretion without real appeal, notwithstanding all the fine words that may appear in the proposed paragraph, and the methods of appeal which follow in the act.
It states that the "Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing...." That is ministerial discretion, and in the exercise of ministerial discretion there is no appeal to a court because no court will substitute its

discretion for that of ministerial exercise of discretion. This is an old axiom of law, and it is only those people who are not versed in law who may believe a court will substitute its discretion for that of a minister if it is properly exercised.
Paragraph 3 reads:
The value for duty of goods imported shall he determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 36 to 41A-
But sections 36 to 41A are nothing but ministerial discretion all the way through. We may agree with what the Government is trying to do, but we quarrel with the way it is trying to do it.
Paragraph 5 reads:
Where the Governor in Council is satisfied, on a report from the Minister, that the application-
This establishes valuations, and the Minister of National Revenue cannot tell me where there is going to be any right of appeal, because following section 37 of the act we come to the sections, starting with No. 41, dealing with appeals to a Dominion Customs Appraiser, one of the Minister's officials.
Is he going to upset the Minister's opinion in the report that is furnished to the Governor in Council? From the Dominion Customs Appraiser it goes to the Deputy Minister. From the Deputy Minister it may go to the Tariff Board, and from the Tariff Board to the Exchequer Court on a point of law-not valuation, not discretion. I defy the Minister to tell me where, in the provisions of 37A, there can be any exercise of law. It is entirely a matter of judgment.
The Governor in Council is possibly one of the highest authorities in the land. Are we going to be led to believe that a Customs Appraiser is going to upset its valuation on an appeal from a competitor? This is to assist not only British goods but others. The terms are general but the valuations are important to people who may be exporting to Canada from other countries. They have a vested interest in these valuations, and so do Canadians.
The Minister of Industry is going to be interested so far as Canadian automobile manufacturers are concerned. Is a Dominion Customs Appraiser going to vary a valuation established by the Governor in Council on recommendation of the Minister? Let us not be nonsensical. Is the Deputy Minister going to do it? The Tariff Board might, but the chances are awfully slim.
Let nobody tell me they are going to go to court. Why, there is not a bit of law to

be exercised at this point and, recalling from memory, the act specifically states under section 43 or 44 that there lies an appeal to the Exchequer Court on a point of law. In other words, it is not a blanket appeal from the decision, yet these were the people who cried to high heaven in 1961 about the exercise of ministerial discretion without appeal. But if you know your Act, if you understand the workings of the Customs Act-not the Customs Tariff Act-you will note that this is the same thing. Plus ga change, plus c'est la meme chose.
I trust some of my colleagues took note of some of the things said by the Minister of Transport. He stood over here on this bide and waxed most indignant. It was something to behold. This was the traducing of all that was fair and aboveboard and right in this country. This was a denial of democracy. This was a denial of the rights of law, that a Minister should have the right to determine a value without appeal. Now these self-same people come to us and say that the Governor in Council can be satisfied on a report from a Minister. This makes a nonsense of what they said and did.
It will be very instructive to see what the majority of the Government party in the other place does on this occasion. Will it block the legislation? On that occasion it saw fit to block it. What I am quarrelling with is the method adopted and the sanctimonious attitude of the Minister's colleagues in 1961 when they objected to the same sort of procedure.

It is a setting of values. The Minister can argue that reducing values is not a setting of values. What is the difference? There is not one iota of an appeal that is meaningful in this regard. With regard to the words I am about to read I should like the Minister to tell us exactly what goods may be affected. For the benefit of hon. Members of

For example, they might be bulldozers or other machinery brought into Canada by the Government of the United States. If they had been used for a while they could be brought in at a lower rate and that rate could be zero. This section 104 may be related to the sections which are headed "value for duty" by cross-reference. If so there would be appeals to the Customs Appraiser, etc. I will have an opportunity to look at that later. What I am primarily concerned about in this section is not what it attempts to achieve but the manner in which the intentions of the Government are carried out. I would simply say that I believe a lot of the things which were said in 1961 by some of the Minister's
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I believe he was a member of the Public Accounts Committee.
No.
I believed the hon. gentleman was, in which case he would know, with respect to the amendments to section 104 that they are specifically as recommended by that Committee.
Thay may be so. I am not a member of the Public Accounts Committee. I have enough to do without being on that Committee.

In joining this discussion on the customs tariff I should like first of all to substantiate what my hon. friend from Edmonton West has said regarding ministerial discretion. My attitude toward this is well known. I recall very clearly what happened in 1961 and the position the Liberal Party took during the debate at that time.
I should like the Minister to explain to the committee how section 37A would operate in connection with the importation of cherries into Canada from the United States, and what value for duty would be established. The season is fast approaching and Canadian cherry producers will suffer severe competition unless some protection is given to them either through import duty provisions or by means of the stabilization act. Possibly the Minister has some observations he can make in this regard.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It was simply a case of the American Gov-vernment moving in a great quantity of dirt-moving machinery that was made in my constituency. This machinery was sent to help establish an American base in Canada. When they had established the base, in accordance with a deal made between the Liberal Government of this country and the American Government the machinery would be thrown on the Canadian market for auction and Canada would be paid 10 per cent for its work in selling the machinery.
The Minister has improved this situation slightly by saying that when this second-hand machinery is sold it will be charged with the duty payable at such rate as may be determined by the Minister. But what rate will be determined by the Minister? This is wide open. The Minister might say, "It is free;

there is no rate on it"; or he might say, "It is at just half the regular rate". It leaves the matter wide open for graft and patronage, in my opinion, because of the way it is set out in the amendment. Mr. Chairman, there are two pieces of information I would like from the Minister. It would not be necessary if he had given a long, detailed explanation when this was introduced, but I do not think he did. One of the questions I would like to ask the Minister is this. Why is it not possible under section 37A to give some indication of a percentage in terms of the gross profit? The reason I ask is that it seems to me that if this clause is designed to assist the British, for example, coming into the Canadian market, the people shipping into the market would be prepared to give some cost figures in regard to production, and then would come the really controversial point as to what was the profit picture. Almost all the British automobile manufacturers, for example, are world-wide agencies to the degree that the manufacturing organizations are in a sense in many cases American subsidiaries. I do not know how you go about tracing profit, and matters like that, in such a situation. That is why it seems to me that if you just leave it as "such amount for gross profit as is deemed reasonable by the Governor in Council" it will, as was pointed out earlier, give a great opportunity for free play. I would like the Minister to tell me why it could not be a figure like 4 per cent, 7 per cent, or something like that.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could deal with the questions that have been raised. First of all dealing with the questions raised by the hon. Member for Edmonton West, of course the matter of the valuation of the particular quantity of goods imported into Canada is always a matter of fact, and a matter which the Dominion Customs Appraiser and the people in my Department try to establish very carefully. I am informed that in connection with the proposed amendment to Section 37, namely the addition of section 37A-* which was the section to which the hon. Member objected-there is an appeal by the Canadian manufacturer if there is the belief that the value established is lower than the cost of production, plus a normal gross profit.
Customs Act
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I might deal with the question raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur.
Is there any right of appeal by the importer?

The appeal is by the person in Canada, the affected industry in Canada.
At this point I might very well deal with the question raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur with regard to the establishing of the amount of gross profit. The valuation which is placed upon the goods may not be less than the cost of production plus gross profit. I do not think it is possible to transscribe into legislation what figure of gross profit should be applied in various industries, because from my experience as an accountant before coming to this House, the amount of gross profit varies a great deal depending on the type of industry concerned.
I should perhaps at this point go back and deal with the various matters raised by my hon. friends opposite. I notice, first of all, that the proposed amendment with regard to bonding was not raised as a factor by any hon. Member. The changes here are changes that were recommended both by the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee. So perhaps I need not deal with those any further. I will go on to deal with the proposed section 37A, which was the main point raised by the hon. Member for Edmonton West. As I mentioned in his absence I have been informed by officials of my department that under section 37A there is the right of appeal if the value which is established by the Minister under this section is lower than the cost of production plus gross profit. In that case a Canadian producer can appeal this matter; I have been informed.
To whom?
He can appeal to the Exchequer Court.
The Minister is aware of section 45 of the Act. It is a point of law, in his opinion?
The opinion of the officials of my department is that it is.
You speak as an accountant, not as a lawyer?

Yes, I am not giving a legal opinion. Section 37A is being added mainly because of the different methods of distribution that exist in a compact country such

June 17, 1965
Customs Act
as Great Britain, and exist in Canada. Section 36 specifies that the value for duty of imported goods shall be the fair market value of like goods when sold for consumption in the country of export under the conditions which are laid down in the section. Under subsection (3), if an exporter is selling to a wholesaler in Canada, while in the home market he sells only to retailers, the value for duty is based on the price to such retailers. Subsection 2(e) (i) provides that if the quantity shipped to Canada is larger than the largest quantity sold for home consumption-that is, in the country of export-those quantities shall be deemed to be the same quantities in determining the value for duty.
The British claim that in certain cases the operation of these two provisions discriminates against the United Kingdom exporter in favour of exporters in other countries. Because of the geographic size of the Canadian market, the lines of distribution in Canada are often longer than in compact countries such as Great Britain. In Canada, for example, goods may pass in turn from the manufacturer to a wholesaler, to a retailer and finally to the consumer, while in Britain the manufacturer often sells to the retailer. Hence the British argue that while they sell in Canada to the same trade level and in similar quantities as, for example, American exporters, the British must, because of the combined effects of section 36 and the anti-dumping law, price their goods as if they were selling in the much more compact British market to a lower level of trade and in smaller quantities. This has raised the value of their goods being imported into Canada. They are thus hard put to compete with other exporters who, because their domestic market is similar in structure to the Canadian one, are allowed to claim trade and quantity discounts denied the British in establishing value for duty under the present law.
In effect, the existing legislation discriminates against certain countries by imposing a higher valuation base than would be obtained if market conditions in those countries were similar to those in other exporting countries. Not only are ordinary duties assessed on the higher values, but in respect of goods of a class or kind made in Canada exporters are prevented from reducing their prices to competitive levels by the threat of our antidumping duty.

[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The proposed new section 37A provides authority to remove these inequities to provide for lowering of values of British goods coming into Canada, while at the same time retaining sufficient safeguards against unfair prices-that is, that there will not be wholesale dumping by people selling in Canada at prices lower than their cost of production, plus the normal gross margin in the trade.
The application of the section will not, of course, be limited to Britain but will also be available to other countries against which the present legislation discriminates. The intention of section 37A is to be relieving. I could inform hon. Members that in discussions which my officials have had with British officials they are very pleased that we have introduced this particular legislation in order to assist them and other such countries in the valuation for duty which is placed on their goods coming into Canada. There has been a very warm reception by the British Board of Trade and the British Government of this particular amendment to the Customs Act.
The other main question which was raised was that raised by the hon. Member for Edmonton West and the hon. Member for Wellington South with respect to section 104 (la). I can tell my hon. friends that this does not apply with respect to cherries. I remember very well, when the cherry producers last year were in great difficulty, that our eminent Minister of Agriculture, in consultation with his other colleagues in the Cabinet, came to the aid of the cherry producers in a manner that has never happened before under any Government in Canada's history, and the cherry producers were very well treated last year.
I wonder whether the Minister could at this point state under what authority payments were made to the cherry growers of Canada.
These were payments allowed the Department of Agriculture under the farm stabilization act.
That was legislation enacted by the previous administration.
Even I admit that some little pieces of legislation passed by the previous administration were good. They provided the instrument and we took advantage of it.

speechtext:
Do not be so modest.

In regard to section 104 (la), the proposed new subsection is designed to give authority to a practice which has been followed by the Department of National Revenue for some time now, both under the previous Government and the present Government, and which would be consistent with the general responsibility for appraisal imposed by the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff. The subsection is intended to deal particularly with disposal in Canada of surplus United States government property, such as equipment used in joint defence installations. Much of this equipment was originally imported free of duty and taxes under appropriate authority, such as tariff item 708, being the property of the United States government. However, when subsequently sold in Canada the goods became liable to the payment of duties in accordance with subsection (1) of section 104 of the Customs Act.
Over the years the Canadian Government has been a party to an agreement with the United States Government providing for the sale in Canada of certain United States surplus goods by an agency of the Canadian Government, namely Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. Under the terms of the agreement the selling price of such goods to the Canadian purchaser is deemed to include duties and taxes. Crown Assets Disposal Corporation remits a certain percentage of that selling price to the Department of National Revenue as representing the duties and taxes applicable. This percentage is a composite rate based on the average rate of duty, and taxes paid on imports from the United States.
Again I reiterate that this has been the practice over a good many years and was a question raised by the Auditor General and discussed by the Public Accounts Committee. Such a composite rate representing both duty and tax is thought to be a logical expedient in view of the special circumstances relating to the disposal of the surplus goods in question. Under normal conditions imported goods are presented to qualified customs officers who have facilities for rating and valuing in accordance with the law. However, the United States surplus goods are often located in remote and inaccessible areas such as D.E.W. line sites in Labrador and the far north of Canada. In addition, a great variety of goods is involved. This combination of circumstances makes it practically impossible to appraise the goods in the normal way without undue expenditure of public funds. That is to say, the cost of sending Customs Apprais-
Customs Act
ers to go and look at the goods disposed of would be far greater than the amount of maximum additional revenue which the Department of National Revenue could realize from such an appraisal.
During the past year the Department's practice was studied by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. The committee in its eighth report to the House on December 7, 1964 recognized the practice as being sensible and practicable.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. When these goods are being disposed of interested bidders are provided with a comprehensive listing of all equipment item by item. Therefore, is it necessary to have inspection of this equipment which is being disposed of, which in many cases the bidders themselves have difficulty seeing?

If one is to consider disposal of used equipment in the far north of Canada, Canadian Customs Appraisers must not only value the goods according to their description but also according to their condition. It had been decided by the previous Government which my hon. friend supported in this House that it is much better to establish a composite rate of duty and apply it to the goods, rather than have Customs Appraisers trail off into the far north, look at the goods and try to establish the value; and the Public Accounts Committee and Auditor General have agreed with this.
However, the Public Accounts Committee did recommend that an amendment be made to the Customs Act or to the Customs Tariff to provide a statutory authority to establish a composite rate to be applied to the proceeds of all sales in Canada of United States government property by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. All we are talking about is the rate of duty which we apply; and it was recommended by the Auditor General and decided by the Public Accounts Committee that such composite rates should be established by statute, which is exactly what we are trying to do by section 104 (la).
Just one question in this regard, and I apologize for displaying ignorance. Was it the fact that previously the full rate of duty was applicable to second hand machinery?

As I understand the situation and have been informed by my departmental officials, for many years, dating back through the administration of the previous Government, the entire term of the Government

Customs Act

No. What has happened in the past is that a composite rate of duty on like goods has been established and applied to all goods being offered by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, and that amount reverts to the Department of National Revenue.

I merely want to ask the Minister a question about the proposal made by the hon. Member for Port Arthur. I think 37A will be greatly improved, from the standpoint of British importers who have suffered serious discrimination in the past, particularly with reference to the import of cars. I think some provision like this is essential to meet this discrimination which they have suffered. The Member for Port Arthur, however, was asking the Minister whether it would not be possible to tie this down a little better, because it says only that the Governor in Council can set an amount equal to the cost of production of the goods plus such amount for gross profit as is deemed reasonable by the Governor in Council. I recognize the Minister's point that you cannot set a specific profit or value of profit margin, but would it be possible to either set a maximum, which would be the cost of production and not more than X percentage of profit, so as to prevent the Governor in Council from adding to the cost of the production of machinery a profit that was so unrealistic that the discrimination could actually continue; or if that is not practical, could the importer have some right of appeal, such as the manufacturer in Canada now has so that he might show that his gross profit was nowhere near the amount that was suggested by the Governor in Council?

First of all, X should indicate that this last provision of the Act goes back to the minimum values which anybody can place on anything which is coming into Canada, or being exported to Canada and sold in this country; that is, the cost of produc-

tion plus the normal gross margin in the country in which it is produced. This gets back to the absolute minimum amount of value that can be placed on any goods that are imported into Canada, without being subject to dumping duty. So the values established for goods coming in from other countries would not ordinarily get back to this cost of production plus gross profit.
This is the argument that the British people have been placing before the Canadian Government, that because their lines of distribution are much confined in that country and they frequently sell manufacturer to retailer, we should vary this system in order to put them in a comparable position with other countries which have lines of distribution such as Canada, where the goods may pass from manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer.
Really the question that is raised is a question of minimum valuation, which is the minimum valuation as I understand the situation under the whole of The Customs Act. The minimum valuation that one can arrive at is the cost of production plus the normal gross margin. This is not arrived at by my Department arbitrarily. If a question is raised with regard to value of duty, an officer of my Department looks into the actual cost of production and gross margins in that particular industry in the particular country. I do not think one could establish arbitrarily by law a gross margin that would apply, because if one takes a look for example at the jewellery industry, and I mention this only as an example, he might find a high gross margin, such as 100 per cent of cost. If one takes a look at other sorts of production in different countries, he might find that the gross margin is only 10 per cent. The fair way is to look at the particular industry in the particular country and apply the gross margin to the particular industry that is involved.
Does the Minister think the right of appeal is impracticable?

Well I did mention this, but I will repeat it. I am not going to give a legal opinion, as I am not a lawyer; but in regard to section 37A my Department officials have indicated to me that the right of appeal is on the side of the importer, or the person in Canada who is being affected in this regard.

But there is no right of appeal for the importer who may feel that the Governor in Council has estimated too high the gross profit, with the consequential result that the valuation for the purposes of duty is much higher in his opinion than it should be.

I think my hon. friend is correct in that regard. This applies generally throughout the Customs Act. If one looks to the Tariff Board, he will find that there are cases of appeals by people importing into the country who have felt the law as it exists has been unfairly applied.
They would not have an appeal against a decision made under section 37A by the Governor in Council. Would there be any right of appeal against such a decision?

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to get myself into the position of giving a legal opinion, and I want to reserve the right to get in touch with my hon. friend to give him the legal opinion of my Department in this regard. I do not wish to attempt to argue the legal rights in respect of appeals.

I should like to ask the Minister one or two questions concerning the suggested amendments to section 104 (la), which relate to the composite rate. As I understand what the Minister has said, these goods will be sold on the basis of a composite rate. In other words, they will be lumped together, for some reason of which we are not clear, and offered for sale on the basis of a composite rate. The question which arises is this. Supposing a small operator has a legitimate use for and wants to buy one piece of machinery such as a dredge, tractor, or some part of the composite group-and I speak with some experience in this regard-will it be possible for him to do so? My experience has been that it is impossible for an individual to purchase just one piece of machinery because the Government prefers to sell a whole lot as a composite group. The Government prefers to make one deal, and the individual is left outside in the cold. He may have a use for and a desire to purchase a particular piece of machinery, but it is sold as part of the composite group. [DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The Minister's intention is to impose a composite rate. I take it from the word "composite" that what he has in mind is to take a whole floor of machinery and lump it all and then somebody will come along and buy the whole thing. Will you please answer that question?

First of all, I should explain that under this section of the Customs Act the Minister of National Revenue is not at all involved in selling the particular goods in question. How they are sold by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation is entirely up to the Corporation. The Department of National
Customs Act
Revenue has nothing to say about this. What we are dealing with in this particular section is securing for the Federal Government out of any ultimate sale the amount of tariff to which the Government is entitled. We do not affect the method of sale or to whom Crown Assets Disposal Corporation sells the particular goods. We are simply saying here that the amount of tariff payable to us will be at a certain rate on the particular amount of goods.
As I mentioned previously, this is a matter which was commented on by the Auditor General. It was also studied by the Public Accounts Committee and it was recommended to the Department of National Revenue that something be put in the Customs Act in order to legalize this method of applying duty. We are not at all involved in the selling of the goods. We have no interest in to whom they are sold or in how tenders are called, or anything else. Our sole interest is to apply a tariff to the goods which is fair in all the circumstances, and which provides for the minimum cost of collection so far as the Federal Government is concerned.

Then you have two Government Departments, the Department of National Revenue and Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, valuing goods. Crown Assets Disposal Corporation usually refers to the appraisal made for duty purposes as a guide in establishing their value and offering the goods to the public.
No.

The Minister says "no". In this legislation there is an open end with regard to what method the Department of National Revenue has to follow in making valuations for duty purposes. At the same time the valuation finds its way into the final price which people are asked to pay to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the fact is that the two are related. I have followed these sales through Crown Assets and they have got to look somewhere in order to get their value. They will send a man out and he will appraise the goods, and in making his appraisal he will take his cue from the value that the Government has already placed on them for duty purposes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer this question by saying that the whole purpose of this section is so that we do not have to go out and appraise goods. The goods are appraised by Crown Assets Dia-

June 17, 1965
Customs Act
posal Corporation and we apply a composite rate of duty to the appraisal placed on them by the vendor. The selling of the goods has nothing to do with the Department of National Revenue. All we want to do is to collect a fair amount of tariff in respect of these goods. We are authorized by this amendment to the section, which is detailed in the bill that will be forthcoming when we complete the resolution, to apply a composite rate of duty rather than applying a rate with regard to each specific item as valued.
Do I understand the Minister to say that you take the appraisal of the goods given to you by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and apply a rate?
Right.

Then there are not two Government organizations making appraisals. What assurance have you that Crown Assets Disposal Corporation will make a proper valuation? What basis do they use in making their appraisal? Is it market value, is it value in use or is it whatever someone is willing to pay? We have been given no guide lines with regard to the definition of value, and how it is arrived at is about as uncertain as trying to pin an eel with a blunt fork. The Government should get down to business and give us something to stand on.

Mr. Chairman, I am not very clear yet on this matter and I should like to ask the Minister a question. When those who bring the machinery into Canada are finished with it, and it is then turned over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the Corporation disposes of it, does the Corporation pay the Department of National Revenue on the basis of the price at which they sold it, or do they value it prior to that time and pay on the basis of that amount?
Mr. Chairman, if there are any other questions perhaps I might deal with them at the same time.

I want to ask the Minister a question. Under this section the composite rate may be such rate as is determined by the Minister. It has been admitted that the Government has been doing this in the past and is now coming to Parliament to legalize a practice that has been going on. I should like to ask the Minister what this rate has been in the past, compared with the regular rate on new equipment?

Mr. Chairman, the composite rate is applied on the selling price, the price at which the goods are actually sold. The composite rate that has been used is 15.25 per cent, I am informed by officials of my Department, and I would think that this rate is determined by taking a group of various assets that are being sold and averaging the rates on all of these assets rather than applying a specific rate to each particular asset.
The rate of 15.25 per cent is levied on the actual selling price?
Yes.
Mr. Chairman, if the Minister does not mind I should like him to tell me whether the 15.25 per cent is on the valuation established by Crown Assets or on the sale price by Crown Assets?
The sale price.

Do those who make the appraisal for Crown Assets Disposal Corporation take into consideration that they can sell the goods at a certain figure, make their appraisal accordingly and then at the same time include within their appraisal the 15.25 per cent? In other words, if Crown Assets valued them any higher they would not be able to sell them.

Mr. Chairman, I am not competent to answer with regard to the basis on which Crown Assets Disposal Corporation may place values on goods. My job as Minister of National Revenue is to collect a reasonable amount of customs tariff on goods which may have come into Canada duty free, or at a small rate of duty, and are then sold within this country. The Department of National Revenue applies a composite rate of duty on the actual selling price of the goods. Our belief, which I think was confirmed by the Public Accounts Committee who looked into the matter, was that we were collecting the amount of duty to which Canada would normally be entitled, and by using the composite rate method rather than proceeding to examine all the goods we were collecting the revenue with the lowest cost to the Government of Canada. The methods used by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation in valuing such goods for tender purposes, and so on, really are not part of the responsibility of the Department of National Revenue.

To return to my original question, why do we not place on this second hand machinery the original duty that would be

appliable to it if it were brought into the country by a private individual? The Public Accounts Committee simply asked that what has been done be legalized, but it did not say this was the right way or right policy.

I would like to think that the Public Accounts Committee, if they thought this was wrong-and I was a Member of it two years ago-would have said they thought it wrong, and said so rather violently. As I explained, under normal conditions goods are presented to qualified customs appraisers in Canada who have facilities for rating them and valuing them in accordance with the law. The U.S. goods which are disposed of in this manner are often located in remote, inaccessible areas such as D.E.W. line sites.
In addition a great variety of goods may be involved in any single disposal. This combination of circumstances makes it practically impossible to appraise the goods in a normal way without undue expenditure of public funds. In other words, it would cost us more money to go and appraise them, and collect the duty than it does to apply a composite rate.

If my memory serves me right there is a condition about the sale of these goods which come primarily from the United States, that they shall not be reimported into the continental United States. In other words, Canada is being used as a dumping ground for this surplus of equipment.
I know of cases where traders have swept up equipment in the Pacific islands and brought it to Alaska where huge auctions are held. Then the equipment is brought into Canada. I disagree with the policy of Crown Assets. The Department of National Revenue is not getting what it should, because these goods are sold in the north on an as is, where is basis, and trucks and tractors can be got practically for a song because of the remoteness of the area and the limited number of purchasers.
With modern methods of transportation it would be much better to bring these goods to a more centralized market site where there would be more competitive bidding and the prices would be higher. I ask the Minister to use his good offices to convince the Minister of Industry that Crown Assets policy is rather shortsighted in this regard.

These goods are brought into Canada primarily for a military purpose. They go through some usage and then they are dumped. There are instances of astute men making 1,000 per cent to 5,000 per cent profit by buying this equipment and transporting it to where there is a good market for the goods.

I would like to assure the hon. Member for Edmonton West that as Minister of National Revenue I am interested in getting everything to which the Canadian Government is entitled out of these goods in the form of customs tariff, and I will bring his useful suggestions to the attention of the Minister of Industry.

If the Minister or anyone else went into the areas where these sales take place they would find discontent among the residents because usually a trader buys the goods for a song. He offers any items he can sell locally to the residents, but transports the rest to another area and the profits are tremendous. It is impossible for the small man to get a crack at this gain through Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. It is all very good to smile, but if the Minister was up there trying to buy this equipment he would find that what I am saying is exactly the truth. If he wants to keep happy and contented people in these areas, he should look at the problem as it exists in them.
I have already indicated that neither I nor my department are involved in the disposal of the goods but I will bring the representations of hon. Members to the attention of the Minister of Industry.

I am thinking along the lines of protection for Canadian manufacturers. This paragraph states that the rate will be such as may be determined by the Minister, and he has said it is based on the actual sales value of whatever equipment might be sold. This may approximate a fire sale, and goods sold at a fire sale, if they are sold in this country, do in effect come in as dumped goods. The rate should be fixed on the reasonable cost of similar goods in Canada, taking into account transportation to the points at which the goods are sold.
In this field Canada is losing revenue, and if the duties were at a higher rate Canada would gain more revenue, o (9:10 p.m.)
Now if they are being undercut by much more, the suggestion is that this might bring about an imbalance in the production of

Canadian manufacturers. That is the suggestion I have to make to the Minister. The fixing of the rate is discretionary and if a rate is fixed on the basis of a selling price alone then it constitutes discrimination against the Canadian manufacturer who is producing goods for the same market and for the same people.

I have one further question to ask with regard to this kind of dumping. If I am wrong in my assumption I hope the Minister will correct me. When the Americans bring in this type of equipment for D.E.W. line operations or construction in Newfoundland, Labrador or wherever it may be, it is my understanding that there is legislation for bidding its re-entry into the United States. Why does not the Canadian Government set up a duty more comparable with the value of the equipment which comes into Canada in this way?

I understand that the primary purpose of this material is national defence. The intention is not to offer these goods for sale on the Canadian market. In many instances, as the hon. Member knows, they are used in the far north where the wear and tear on goods and machinery is extremely heavy. The sole purpose of this provision in the legislation is to carry out the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee that the Minister be authorized to apply a composite rate of duty-15.25 per cent- rather than send somebody out to try to value these things as used.

The Minister has referred to the value of this equipment as "used". Is he aware of the fact that much of this material is re-sold before it is ever put to use? This was the situation during the years between the end of the war and 1957, and it is still going on at the present time.

I should like to ask the Minister, or the Minister in charge of Crown Assets, whether he would discuss the possibility of selling these goods by public auction rather than to individual traders. It seems to me it would give a better chance to the little fellow if this material were sold by auction rather than holus-bolus for a lump sum. In addition, I believe the Department of National Revenue would get more money. The small buyer, in turn, would get an opportunity to purchase equipment at a reasonable price and everyone in the area where these sales take place would be in a better frame of mind.

I make this suggestion despite the fact that the person sitting behind the Minister of National Revenue continues to laugh and smile as though he knew something about what goes on in these areas, though I think he is as dumb as the dumbest person could possibly be in regard to matters of this kind.
I rise merely to make the suggestion that if the Minister of Agriculture were put in charge of the disposal of this equipment he would surely be happy about the results he could get.

Is it paid by the purchaser who bids on the equipment or does the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation pay it to the Department of National Revenue out of the over-all sum which the purchaser bids? Or does the purchaser pay what he bids for the equipment, plus an additional sum in duty?
I am subject to correction but I believe it is paid out of the over-all sum. The bid is made and 15.25 per cent of it automatically goes to the Department of National Revenue.
In that case the purchaser would be paying no duty as an individual.
That is correct.

the information for the trade including franchises, bids, tenders and all the other things that are of common interest. Although I have more substantial comments to make on this particular paragraph this seems to me to be an anomaly, the kind of paradox we keep encountering with this particular government and Minister of Finance in office-on the one hand Canadian nationalism, the Canadian Development Corporation, the cry "Let us save our Canadian insurance companies and banks"; and on the other hand the naturalization of Time and Reader's Digest.
