Paragraph 5 seems to me to have no real planning for the future in terms of certain developments which might take place. I should like the Parliamentary Secretary to note that not too long ago a number of representatives of the churches which put out publications held an annual meeting in Ottawa and lobbied the Government from the point of view that their publications deserved and merited Government advertisements. Customs Tariff
editorial content, to get their circulation up, and so on. There is nothing regrettable about this particular trend, but I would point out that religious publications are specifically exempted under this particular item.

Perhaps I might begin by saying that a significant amount of magazine advertising directed to Canadians is originated by companies which operate outside of Canada or by the foreign affiliates of Canadian firms. That circulation may be directed to one region of the United States or to Canada. This is a result of the fact that many American mass circulation magazines also circulate in Canada on a very large scale.
What is envisaged is that if a particular issue-I emphasize the word "a"-is found to be a split run or regional edition containing advertisements directed to Canada, future issues of the publication will be denied entry. This makes it possible for the proprietors of the publications in question to make any changes necessary in order to avoid the prohibition. The Department of National Revenue
June 17. 1965

will, of course, be getting in touch with all known publishers who might be affected so as to give them every opportunity to make such adjustments in their advertising patterns as may be necessary. That covers the first portion of this item.
The second portion relates to the practice of inserting in advertisements in mass circulation United States magazines which are sold in Canada the address of the Canadian agent or supplier of the products advertised. The O'Leary Commission recommended that no magazines be allowed to enter Canada which contain such advertising. We have come to the conclusion that such a measure would work a hardship in certain cases. There are some products which it is unreasonable to expect would be advertised in Canada in any other way, such as goods which are used only in certain professions or trades, or products which are sold in very limited quantity. Accordingly, it is proposed that all magazines entering Canada be allowed to have a minimum amount of such advertising. It is expected it will be relatively easy for foreign periodicals which circulate in Canada to adjust their advertising arrangements in such a way as to make it unnecessary to invoke this prohibition. maintopic: REDISTRIBUTION-ONTARIO-PUBLICATION OF MAPS IN WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS
REDISTRIBUTION-ONTARIO-PUBLICATION OF MAPS IN WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the time allotted to me tonight to bring before the House a matter regarding the failure of the Government to contact the Weekly Newspapers of Ontario in the publication of the maps and data regarding the Redistribution Act.
My point deals with discrimination against an important part of the Fourth Estate, the most important part of our news media in Ontario, the weekly newspapers.
This Government has again shown its capacity for downright stupidity, and has portrayed its usual ingrained arrogance in what has been allowed to happen this week with respect to advertisements under the Redistribution Act. The placing of approximately $250,000 worth of advertising exclusively in the columns of the big dailies is an indication of a certain complete consideration or, shall I say, Mr. Speaker, "value received", vis-a-vis, the daily papers to keep them quiet and clear of criticism regarding many evident gerrymanderings in the political redistribution. A good, timely cartoon, in this regard, would show the right hon. Prime Minister and the Secretary of State hurrying by the office of a small weekly paper, with furtive glances, on their way to their destination, the office of a large "daily" to which they intend to give all the business.
I submit that the advertising done under the Redistribution Act need not have cost a quarter of a million dollars; it needed to entail, possibly, only paying for the publishing of the maps. As for the other information concerning the boundaries of each constituency, any newspaper, weekly or daily, would be glad to publish this information free of charge as news. One weekly publisher in my riding wanted to publish this information as news and had to telephone Ottawa at his own expense to get the details. Another weekly publisher in Northumberland County had to do the same, while the Government was paying many thousands of dollars and giving full service, plus advance notice, to their favourites, the dailies.
June 17, 1965	COMMONS
Mr. Speaker, there are at least 215 weekly newspapers in Ontario, with a combined circulation of almost 600,000. The people who read these newspapers, a combined total of at least two million people, or one-third of our population, are people who either cannot afford, or do not choose, to pay the larger subscription rate which a daily naturally, must charge. And so these people look forward to getting their news via the local weekly.
I have no criticism to make of the dailies whatsoever, as to their valuable services. I believe that they have given value for the money which is spent in accordance with their rates, though of course those rates are much higher than the rates of the weekly papers. I submit that the readers of these weekly papers, 600,000 families, or at least two million people, have also been ignored and discriminated against by this Government. Every voter in Canada has the right to know the particulars of the redistribution of his or her constituency, and has the right to be reached. Moreover, every voter has the right to appeal the decisions of the Redistribution Commission if he wishes. This Government is, by its action, or lack of action, discriminating against hundreds of thousands of rural voters who subscribe to weekly papers only.
I have irrefutable proof of this in an example which I will cite in my riding where one rural route which was checked and assessed had 197 drops. Only eight of these drops take a daily newspaper. On that rural route last Tuesday, the day of publication of the Redistribution Commission information, eight families were fully informed regarding the future of their constituency while 189 families were left completely uninformed in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, the Ontario weekly newspaper editors protest the failure of this Government to recognize them as part of our news media. No one had any idea that the whole Province of Ontario would be treated in this way at a high cost per entry in the daily papers. I would give another example: The smallest daily in Ontario received this business, yet its circulation is only one-half that of a weekly paper five miles away.
There is another point, Mr. Speaker. That is the silence of the backbench Ontario Liberal Members, supporters of this Government, which demonstrates their complete agreement with and concurrence in this ludicrous policy which, of course, emanates from their masters, the Cabinet. This is

The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) answered this question in a roundabout way when he said that the suggestion made by the hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), who raised this matter last Monday, had been communicated to the Commission. I have since been informed that the Chairman of the Commission has been contacted on behalf of the editors of the Ontario weeklies and says he will take direction from Parliament in this matter.
I note that the Secretary of State, as reported at page 2334 of Hansard of June 14, in answering a question posed by the hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) gave the ridiculous answer that these Commissions are not agencies of the Crown and that they are not accountable to the Crown. maintopic: EDUCATION-STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO IMPROVEMENTS IN PLAN
EDUCATION-STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO IMPROVEMENTS IN PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) tabled in the House a report with reference to the Canada student loan plan. This report dealt mainly with the administrative matters that have occupied the attention of the Federal-Provincial group. Yesterday in reply to a question which I asked concerning the student loan program, the Minister answered:
It may be that at some appropriate time it will be desirable to bring in amending legislation, but I have no plans to do so at the moment.
This is the part of the Minister's answer with which I was dissatisfied and is the reason I am making a very few comments tonight. I would submit that some legislative provisions are needed and should be provided immediately so that students can make their plans for this fall when they enter university. The student loan plan is deficient in some matters of principle and not just in administrative matters. First, Mr. Speaker, I believe the plan should be expanded so that it is in the nature of a bursary loan plan under which a student who has shown exceptional promise in the school year and who has obtained a student loan would have the right to a write-off of part of the loan. This would recognize ability in the student who ordinarily might not have gone to university because of the financial situation and who might turn out to be a good student who would make a real effort in his studies.
They are people who I think should be encouraged. That is why I suggest there should be a bursary type of loan granted, and it should be granted right away. I would suggest that it take the form of cancellation of part of the debt incurred at the end of the school year, perhaps to the extent of 25 per cent for those people with a clear pass, and perhaps to the extent of a further 25 per cent for those in the top quarter of their class.

DEBATES	June 17, 1965
Another group who have not been covered by the plan are graduate students, and those students who have taken their full term and are going on to postgraduate work. I think the ceiling should be eliminated in respect of those people when they go into graduate work so that they can continue their studies. It might be said that this will not take place for a few years; but these people should know now whether they are going to run out of money before they have finished their work. I think it is essential that there be a provision made for graduate students who, in the normal course, will go beyond what is allowed under the loan plan. This is something which should also be attended to right away.
Finally, there is the group whose graduation is followed by an apprenticeship. This group comprises medical students, law students and similar persons, some of whom, I understand, have made a presentation to the Minister on this very point. While they may have graduated they are also engaging upon a further year of study. During this year they are paid only subsistence wages, if anything. They should not be required to start repayment of their loan or to commence paying interest on it, at least until their apprenticeship has been completed and another six months has passed.
There are other improvements in the loam plan which have come up in the past year and which have been suggested in various briefs to the Government. It is not sufficient at this time for the Minister merely to say that we are catching up with some of the administrative problems in relation to this plan and that perhaps at some time in the future we will reconsider the basics. I would much prefer to hear him say that the Government will look at this student loan plan seriously and make the amendments which are really necessary.

maintopic: EDUCATION-STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO IMPROVEMENTS IN PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in regard to the loan plan let me say at once, whether improvements should or should not be brought in, that the number of students assisted to date, or as of April 1, is 41,284. So in my respectful submission it does provide a very valuable service.
Several Federal-Provincial Conferences of officials have been held to discuss ways and means of improving the operations of the plan. At the last full Federal-Provincial meeting held on March 29, agreement on improvements was reached on those areas where it was felt that experience had demonstrated the lack of
June 17, 1965

harmony in the practices being followed. Full details of these arrangements were included with the statement of the Minister of Finance, which was incorporated as Appendix "A" in Hansard of June 11.
The purpose of these agreed arrangements is to ensure that the plan is available to students on as standard and consistent a basis as possible in all participating provinces. As hon. Members are aware the Canada Student Loans Act makes available to students, by virtue of the federal Government guarantee, a source of financing through the commercial banks and other approved lenders. All questions relating to the eligibility of students for loans and the designation of educational institutions which students may attend with the help of a student loan are administered by experienced provincial authorities who are designated for purposes of the Act by participating provinces. Co-ordination among the provinces concerning their administrative practices is not an explicit requirement of the Act, but of course does much to facilitate its purposes and objectives. No changes in the legislation are required to implement the type of arrangements that have recently been worked out. It may be that as more experience is gained with the plan it will prove desirable to bring in amending legislation.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I will convey the remarks of the hon. Member to the Minister. I must, however, tell him that at the present time there are no plans to make any amendments.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-SPEECH BY FORESTRY MINISTER RESPECTING WHEAT BOARD
AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-SPEECH BY FORESTRY MINISTER RESPECTING WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss a matter of national importance and urgency. It arises out of the unwarranted and scurrilous attack made on the Canadian Wheat Board on June 11 at Drummondville in the province of Quebec by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve). This in itself is a serious matter, but when it is coupled with the deliberate result of driving a wedge between farmers in separate parts of this nation, then I say it is encouraging the destruction of Canadian unity and purpose. That is not something new in the Ministry opposite.
Indeed, I recall recently when farmers from Ontario and some parts of Quebec came to the Chateau Laurier at Ottawa. I recall the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) at that time referring to the hon. Member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) by
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion name, indicating that he would not consider representations from that particular quarter because he thought it might challenge the interests of farmers in Eastern Canada. Again, this same kind of practice drove a wedge between the farmers of different parts of this country.
Of course, we all know it was the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who, during the election campaign of 1963, travelled through other parts of Canada stating that if he was elected he would do for them what John Diefenbaker had done for Western Canada. That tactic was employed by the Prime Minister, that man who was billed by his Party as a man who cares. I ask you, Sir, where the search for unity and purpose of this country is when the men in the ministerial benches opposite go about making statements such as those which have been made.
I have before me the text of the speech delivered by the Minister of Forestry, and I must say that for the most part this is fiction and prejudice, and not much else. These remarks echo the stand taken by the grain brokers of Eastern Canada. This is the old story of these particular interests which have controlled the distribution of feeds and grains in Central and Eastern Canada. This is the old story of these people challenging the efficiency and purpose of the Canadian Wheat Board. This is the old story of these people attacking the orderly method of marketing grain as being the source of their trouble.
I contend that it is a much different matter to have a Minister of the Crown who is one of the three Ministers charged with the responsibility for agriculture taking up this particular cry. The question must be asked, why this alliance of Ministry and grain brokers at this particular time. It seems to me that in respect of this whole matter which reputedly was supposed to deal with feed grain, the Minister is more interested in the brokers and the grain trades than in the farmers.
What does the Minister mean by juggling of the Wheat Board quota; and I should like the Parliamentary Secretary opposite to give an answer, because that is a serious charge and it should be substantiated or withdrawn. What does the Minister mean by adjusting interim payments? Has this situation developed during the period the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has been charged with the responsibility of the Wheat Board operation? I remember a former Minister of
2696	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Agriculture in a former Liberal Government, the late James G. Gardiner, and the adjustment he made just prior to an election campaign. Is the Minister of Forestry suggesting that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce is indulging in the same type of tactic at this particular time in directing interim payments from the Canadian Wheat Board?
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
The Minister has charged that interim payments have been adjusted. This is a serious charge and I contend that it should be withdrawn. The Minister charges that the Board has regulated the allotment of box cars in such a way as to bring about an artificial rationing of feed grain availabilities. This is not only a serious charge but a mischievous one and it should be withdrawn. All of the evidence I can find refutes the Minister's statement in that regard, and the figures of the Canadian Wheat Board show that this is not the case at all.
I know that the Minister, the Parliamentary Secretary and others across the way have boasted about what they did with regard to the feed grain situation last year and the supplies they laid in in Eastern positions. During the period since then the fluctuations in price have been greater than ever before.
The Minister has charged that the Wheat Board operations have resulted in erratic production of feed grains. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that charge is unworthy of the Minister and the Government opposite. The annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board shows that yields have fluctuated from a high of 46.2 bushels per acre in 1956 to a low of 25.2 bushels per acre in 1961. The fluctuation in barley yields has been equally respondent to weather conditions. In the matter of feed wheat grades I ask the Parliamentary Secretary, what can the Canadian Wheat Board do about rust, frost or moisture content?
The Minister went on to say that in Eastern Canada the acreage sown to feed grains is constantly diminishing. It is natural for that to take place when the demand for improved pasture is as great and as economically sound in eastern Canada as it is today. When you consider the price levels of feed grains from Western Canada over the last 10, 12 or 20 years you cannot help but realize that throughout the period right up to the present time these grains have generally been sold by the Canadian Wheat Board at price levels that cannot be touched by producers in other parts of Canada.
I want to conclude by saying that the Government has been guilty of gross negligence
DEBATES	June 17. 1965
in failing to take action with regard to the provision of feed grains for the farmers of Eastern Canada, and to try to place the blame on the Canadian Wheat Board is an action that is unworthy of any Member of the Government.
Mr, B. S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Forestry: Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation to the hon. Member for having brought this important matter to the attention of the House. I am confident that it was not the intention of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) to cast any aspersions on the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board.
I think I can speak for the Government and for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) in particular, who is directly responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, in saying that no one has expressed greater confidence in the Board than have the Government, and especially the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is a matter of very great pride to all Canadians that the orderly marketing of grain in western Canada is in such competent hands. The Wheat Board is envied by other nations throughout the world, which wish that they had marketing agencies that could do the job the Canadian Wheat Board has done for the West and for Canada generally.
This agency was established, of course, for the purpose of bringing about the orderly marketing of grain. Certain responsibilities were placed on the Board by statute and the Board has discharged those responsibilities to its very great credit and to the credit of the country as a whole. I am confident that when the Minister of Forestry was speaking in Eastern Canada it was not his intention, nor would it be the wish of the Government, to cast any reflection on the excellent operation that has been conducted throughout the years by the Canadian Wheat Board. Grain is a very important commodity in Canadian exports and the orderly handling of this product is of national importance.
So, I can say on behalf of the Government and the Minister of Forestry, it was not his intention in any way to cast any reflections but to express confidence in the Canadian Wheat Board and to hope that their operation would continue to be as successful in the future as it has been in the past.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.32 p.m.
